<meta>This is the title page of the 1927 edition of the Ghayat al-Hakim, edited by Hellmut Ritter. It establishes the scholarly foundation for the text known in the West as the Picatrix.</meta>

### The Book of the

# Goal of the Wise
# and the Most Deserving of the Two Results to be Brought Forward
<note>original: "Ghayat al-Hakim wa-Ahaqq al-Natijatayn bi-l-Taqdim." This is the famous medieval grimoire on astral magic and alchemy, later translated into Latin as the "Picatrix."</note>

## Attributed to Abu al-Qasim Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti
<note>Maslama al-Majriti (d. 1007 AD) was a renowned Andalusian mathematician and astronomer from Madrid. While the text is attributed to him, modern scholars believe it was likely written by a different author in the mid-11th century.</note>

->Edited by<-

## H. Ritter
<note>Hellmut Ritter (1892–1971) was a preeminent German orientalist who produced this definitive critical edition of the Arabic text.</note>

---

->Augustin Press in Glückstadt and Hamburg<-
->Year 1927<-

# Table of Contents: Articles and Chapters

## The First Article: Containing Seven Chapters

(1) On the excellence of wisdom <note>Arabic: *al-hikma*; refers to both philosophy and the hidden sciences</note> .......................................... 3
(2) On the true nature of magic .......................................... 6
(3) On the reality of the celestial sphere and its essence ................................... 11
(4) On universal proportions and celestial subjects for the construction of talismans <term>talismans: objects inscribed with astrological symbols intended to draw down celestial power</term> .................. 14
(5) On examples of proportions for placing talismans required for their construction .......... 26
(6) On the human rank and how it corresponds to the Macrocosm <note>The "Macrocosm" refers to the universe as a whole, reflecting the "Microcosm" of the human being</note> .................. 42
(7) On existing things and their origins, including obscure meanings written by the scholars ............. 51

## The Second Article: Containing Twelve Chapters

(1) By what means one may attain this science ........................... 54
(2) On celestial images and references to their symbols in the movement of the spheres ......... 58
(3) On the influences of the higher planets and the misfortune <note>referring to "malefic" astrological aspects</note> of the Sun and Moon ............. 63
(4) On the movement of the celestial spheres ........................................ 78
(5) On the division of this world among all nations and the portion of each group within it ......... 80
(6) On the essence of specific properties, the forms of gifts from the planets, and the manner of receiving their actions ... 86
(7) On the use of the positions of the Categories <note>referring to the Aristotelian Categories</note> in the art of talismans and how they are incorporated ... 96
(8) On the ranks of natural matters and their appendages ........................... 101
(9) On formal examples of the conjunction of the fixed stars ..................... 104
(10) On the stones and engraved images belonging to the planets ..................... 106
(11) On the images of the faces of the Zodiac signs and their effects .............................. 124
(12) On the images of the degrees <note>Arabic: *darajan*; the 360 degrees of the zodiac</note>, their effects, and their influences according to the school of the Indians; and a discussion on the nature of thought and the attraction of celestial powers according to their school, with a portion of their magical works ............. 133

### The Third Treatise: Its Twelve Chapters

(1) On the portions <note>astrological dignities or influences</note> of the planets within the three kingdoms of nature <note>original: "al-muwalladat al-thalatha" referring to minerals, plants, and animals</note> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 149
(2) On the portions of the Zodiac signs . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 157
(3) On the periods of the planets and their forms; the distribution of their garments and incenses; the periods of the faces <note>decanates</note> of the Zodiac signs used in magical operations; the properties found in the climates <note>latitudinal zones</note> due to their alignment with the planets; and the specific properties of various lands . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 160
(4) On the secret known only to those firmly rooted in knowledge . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 169
(5) On the specific properties assigned to animals and necessary fragments of knowledge; and how to attract <term>spirituality</term> <note>original: "ruhaniyya," referring to the celestial or planetary spirits</note> through total planetary correspondence . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 177
(6) On the art of attracting spirituality known as the "Perfect Nature" according to the school of Aristotle and Hermes; and the meaning and form of the <term>talisman</term> <note>original: "tilsam"</note> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 187
(7) On attracting the powers of the planets and communing with them by standing before them; and the distribution of the effects of actions according to the school of the Sabians <note>a religious group from Harran known for star worship</note> through forms, sacrifices, prayers, incenses, and celestial proportions . . . . . . . . . . . 195
(8) On the veneration of the Nabataeans for the two planets, the Sun and Saturn, and the manner of their communion with them . . . . . . . . . . . . 229
(9) On attracting the powers of the planets individually; the names of the spiritualities of those powers placed toward the six directions; and their employment according to what Aristotle mentioned . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 233
(10) On the making of spiritual <term>niranj</term> <note>original: "nayranjiyya," referring to sorcerous charms or illusions</note> beads and compounds to repel harmful works, taken from Aristotle; and the authentic findings from the science of Kaynas the Indian regarding magical talismanic charms, feedings, incenses, perfumes, and oils, and how to undo their effects once they have taken hold of a subject . . . . . . . . . . . 242
(11) On charms for various purposes taken from a group of the ancients; on illusionism, the transformation of essences, and the appearance of diverse forms according to one's will; and on charms that induce sleep, lethargy, death, or repel poisons . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 264
(12) On scientific testaments and subtle points . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 282

### The Fourth Treatise: Its Nine Chapters

(1) On the drawing of lights and the reception of emanation from the First Cause down to the lower beings; a discussion on the reality of the spiritual essence and the corporeal essence and their quiddity; and the reality of the Intellect, its divisions, and its quiddity, as well as the reality of the Soul and its quiddity . . . . . . . . . . . . . 286
(2) On attracting the spirituality of the Moon's powers when it enters the beginnings of the Zodiac signs and dispersing its powers into the earth according to the school of a group of Kurds and Abyssinians; and the making of the seven <term>qalantariyat</term> <note>likely a specific type of talismanic or ritual object</note> and their fasts according to the school of a group of the people of India . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 295
(3) On the mention of the Egyptians <note>original: "al-Qibt," the Copts</note> and the hidden secrets they possess, and some of their symbols in this result . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 309
(4) On extracting the core insights and subtle points from the words of the masters of this art, to be used as an aid in attaining this result . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 319
(5) On the enumeration of the ten sciences that produced these two results . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 333
(6) On the craft of planetary incenses, which is among the greatest secrets of India for general effects, and the compounds that follow in this matter . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 341
(7) On what Abu Bakr ibn Wahshiyya translated regarding the magical works and talismans of the Nabataeans . . . . . . . 350
(8) On the effects of things that act through their specific properties . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 396
(9) On composite talismans of specific properties extracted from the book found in the temple of Saranidus <note>possibly a corruption of a Greek name like Serenus or a legendary figure</note> and from the book of Cleopatra, along with the testaments that follow it . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 405

# In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Praise be to God, from whose light the veils of concealment are illuminated, and from whose might the wonders of destiny flow. To Him all traces lead, and by His command night and day alternate. He is the bringer of things into existence after their non-existence, the originator of creatures and the changer of their blessings. He is the Ordainer, the Creator of every being; He is neither mingled with things nor distinct from them. Attributes do not encompass Him, darkness does not overtake Him, descriptions do not exhaust Him, and accidents do not befall Him. May God bless the Master of the Messengers and the Seal of the Prophets, upon whom the Book was revealed in a clear Arabic tongue—and indeed, it is found in the scriptures of the ancients—and upon his righteous and pure family, and grant them much peace until the Day of Judgment.

As for what follows: O seeker, enticed by diving into the <term>science of the philosophers</term> <note>refers to "falsafa," the Hellenistic tradition of philosophy and science</note>, looking into their secrets, and searching for the wonders they immortalized in their books: know that the motive that moved me to compose this book—which I have named *The Goal of the Wise* <note>original: "Ghayat al-Hakim"</note> and *The Most Deserving of the Two Results to be Put Forward*—is what occurred to me during the composition of the book I wrote previously, which I named *The Rank of the Wise* <note>original: "Rutbat al-Hakim"</note>. My composition of this book began in the year 343 <note>954-955 CE</note> upon my completion of the revision of the book *The Rank of the Wise*, and I finished it at the end of the year 348 <note>959-960 CE</note>. My motivation for writing it was what I saw most people of our time searching for regarding the matter of...

...talismans and the various arts of magic, yet they do not know what they seek, nor which path they intend to follow. Their lives have been exhausted in pursuit of a goal from which they have been barred because the Sages concealed it. They refrained from revealing it due to the potential for the world’s destruction and ruin—and God forbids such a thing, out of concern for the well-being of His world. For this reason, the Sages constructed the <term>temple edifices</term> <note>original: "al-barabi," referring to ancient Egyptian temples or monuments believed to hold occult secrets</note> and placed within them engravings and images to alert and sharpen the intellect. They immortalized what they recorded in books through symbols and <term>riddles</term> <note>original: "al-ta‘miyat," referring to encoded or encrypted text</note> so that none but a Sage like themselves might understand. Amidst this, they provided benefit and clarified the secrets for those who could comprehend their meaning.

Thus, I saw fit to disseminate and explain the obscured path of this "result" called <term>Simya</term> <note>a branch of magic focusing on natural forces and celestial influences; often called "The Alchemy of Images"</note>. I shall clarify what the Sages hid regarding this magical result, just as we previously did for the <term>Alchemical Result</term> <note>original: "al-natija al-san‘awiyya," referring to the "Great Work" of physical alchemy</note>. I have divided this book into four treatises, as we did in *The Rank* <note>referring to the author's other famous work, "Rutbat al-Hakim" (The Rank of the Sage)</note>, with each treatise restricted to a number of chapters.

The first treatise consists of seven chapters—this number is intentional, as the <term>fast-moving planets</term> <note>the seven traditional celestial bodies: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> are seven. The first chapter concerns the nobility of Wisdom. In this first treatise, I will also mention celestial proportions, the nature of celestial ratios used when constructing talismans, and how the planets cast their rays upon the <term>traveler</term> <note>likely referring to the moon or a specific celestial recipient in a ritual</note>. Along with this, I will present obscure meanings that the Sages kept hidden out of possessiveness and a desire to protect them, placed here at the beginning of the treatise.

The second treatise is on celestial images and their actions, explaining the secrets of their workings that the Sages concealed, and providing examples of how magic is <term>borrowed</term> <note>channeled or derived</note> into this world—called the <term>World of Generation and Corruption</term> <note>the earthly realm where things are born, change, and decay</note>—from the celestial world <note>original: "the world of the ether"</note>. It also explains the reason that led Plato to speak of the <term>unification of forms</term>.

The third treatise concerns the shares of the planets in the <term>three offspring</term> <note>the three kingdoms of nature: minerals, plants, and animals</note>, for there is nothing in the world of generation and corruption capable of receiving magical work except them. The <term>elements</term> <note>original: "al-istiqsat"</note> are impossible to work with directly as they are fluid and prone to constant change; thus, only these three remain. I shall mention the temperament of some in relation to others, so that magical works may be targeted through them, using elemental heat or natural heat. These are transferred either through incense used for fumigation, or through things intended for the stomach, such as decoctions or drinks.

The fourth treatise is on the magic of the Kurds, the Nabateans, and the Abyssinians, including examples of <term>mechanical tricks</term> <note>original: "al-hiyal al-sihriyya," often referring to automata or stage magic</note>, which are the finest types of magic. I shall complete this objective as is required, without stinginess or concealment. I ask God for help in completing what we have intended, for He is the Master of that, and with His help, I begin.

<meta>This page continues a metaphysical treatise on the nature of the "First Cause" (God) and the hierarchy of existence. The text flow suggests that the column transcribed as the second block in the OCR (the right-hand column of the manuscript) actually precedes the first block (the left-hand column). The author describes the First Cause as incorporeal, self-sufficient, and the source of all unity and truth, then transitions into an ethical and spiritual praise of Wisdom (Philosophy) as the means to return to this divine origin.</meta>

...for things below them. The First is the cause of what is below it, and there is no cause above it. He knows how the lower beings ascend to one another until they terminate at the First. Then, He knows how the Divine Governance <margin>3</margin> (<term>tadbir</term>—the orderly management of the universe) begins from the First and is received by all existents in their proper order until it reaches the very last of them.

This is Wisdom in reality. What then do you think of this path, O seeker? Through Wisdom—may God strengthen you—one finds a majestic and vast expanse; seeking it is both a religious duty and a virtue. This is because it illuminates the intellect (<term>‘aql</term>) and the soul (<term>nafs</term>) with the eternal, <margin>6</margin> beautiful Light when they seek it. It leads them to renounce this decaying, fading world once they understand its true meaning and vitality, and it makes them long to transition to that high and exalted world which is their starting point, their place of return, their origin, and their final resting place. There, God shall comfort them <margin>9</margin> and reveal to them the nature of the Cause of the world and its effect, and the reason why the Cause manifests the effect. Wisdom is the intermediary between the two, so that they may know with necessary certainty that God Almighty is the Cause of the world and the world is His effect. The reason [for creation] is His making them worship Him through their knowledge of Him and their acknowledgment of His existence, as the Almighty said:<sup>a)</sup> <margin>12</margin> "And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me" <note>original: "wa-ma khalaqtu al-jinna wa-l-insa illa li-ya‘budun"; Surah 51:56</note>, meaning "to know Me." He protects them and provides for them so they might thank and praise Him. He makes miserable whomever He wills and grants happiness to whomever He intends, keeping those He loves with Him in bliss that never perishes.

Wisdom has three essential characteristics: it grows and never decays, it shines and never fades, <margin>15</margin> and it manifests itself to be contemplated without being distant. It also has three governing powers: it restrains [from evil], it disciplines, and it does not turn toward those who desire to abandon it.

...the proximate [causes] of things that have causes. This is achieved by being certain of their existence and knowing what they are and how they are. Even though they are numerous, they ascend in an orderly fashion to a single Existent who is the cause <margin>3</margin> of those distant things and the proximate things below them. That One is the First in reality. His subsistence does not depend on the existence of anything else; rather, He is self-sufficient, <margin>6</margin> needing no existence from another. Indeed, it is impossible for Him to derive existence from any other source. He cannot be a body at all, nor can He exist within a body. His existence is a unique kind of existence, distinct from that of all other beings. He shares no common essence with them; <margin>9</margin> if there is any shared terminology, it is in name only (<term>homonymous</term>—sharing a name but not a definition), not in the actual meaning understood by that name. He can only be one, and He is the One in reality. He is the one who bestowed upon all other beings the unity by which we are able to say of every existent that it is "one." He is the First Truth <margin>12</margin> (<term>al-Haqq</term>—The Real) who grants reality to everything else, while His own reality is self-sufficient. It is impossible to conceive of a perfection greater than His, let alone for such a thing to exist. No existence is more complete than His, no reality more profound than His, and no unity more perfect than His. Furthermore, He knows how <margin>15</margin> all other beings derived existence and reality from Him, as well as the portion of existence, reality, and unity allotted to each. He knows how the various causes derived their causality. He knows the ranks of all existents: some are first, some are middle, and some are last. The last have causes but are not causes for anything below them. The middle existents are those that have a cause before them and are themselves causes...

<meta>This page transitions from the general praise of Wisdom to the specific technical definitions of logic and the occult sciences. The author connects the "Result" (the outcome of spiritual or intellectual work) to the logical "Conclusion" of a syllogism, and then pivots to a technical discussion of Magic, Talismans, and Alchemy.</meta>

Know that this "result" <note>Arabic: *natija*; in logic, this refers to the "conclusion" of a syllogism</note> which we are in the process of uncovering would have no existence were it not for the existence of Wisdom. The Sages were right to call it a "result," for among the masters of logic, the result is the fruit of the syllogism <note>Arabic: *qiyas*; the standard method of deductive reasoning</note> and is the finest element within the premises. The purpose of establishing these two results was nothing other than to urge the pursuit of knowledge. This cannot be attained except by the Sage who has mastered all the branches of Wisdom in their proper ranks. Thus, the status of these two results at the end of Wisdom is like the status of the conclusion in a syllogism, which is the finest part of the premises. Understand this, for I have explained a wondrous secret to you.

Know that the result is the fruit of the two premises, which together are called a "coupling." When they produce a result, they are called a "collector," or in the language of the Greeks, a **syllogism** <note>original: *saljumus*, a transliteration of the Greek *syllogismos*</note>. A premise consists of a **subject** and a **predicate**. The subject is what the grammarians call the "starting noun" (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is the "news" (*khabar*). The "news" is that which may be described as true or false. The subject and predicate are the "attribute" and the "subject of attribution"... <note>The text indicates a missing portion (lacuna) here</note> a statement that is neither limited nor defined. This is because all statements are either not limited or defined, or they are limited, or they are defined. The "declarative statement" is what is used in logical propositions; other types of speech, according to the logicians, are not used—such as commands, inquiries, questions, and vocatives—because they cannot be judged as true or false. What we have said requires a lengthy explanation that would diverge from our purpose, so let whoever wishes seek it from its proper sources.

<column-break/>

Everything that has bewitched the intellects and to which souls have submitted—including all speech and actions—carries the sense of wonder, submission, listening, and approval. It is something difficult for the mind to perceive, and its causes are hidden from the misguided. This is because it is a **divine power** using preceding causes established for its perception; it is a science of obscure perception. 

Part of it is also practical, for its subject is "spirit within spirit," and this is **Niranj** <note>a term for phantasmagoria or prestigious sorcery</note> and illusionism. In contrast, the subject of a **Talisman** is "spirit within a body," and the subject of **Alchemy** is "body within a body." In short, Magic is that whose cause is hidden from most minds and whose derivation is difficult to deduce.

The reality of the **Talisman** <term>tilsam: an object inscribed with astrological symbols to exert influence</term> is that its name is its own reverse: it is the **Subjugator** <note>In Arabic script, T-L-S-M (طلسم) reversed is M-S-L-T (مسلط, *musallit*), meaning "one who is given authority/power over another"</note>. This is because it is made of the essences of subjugation and domination. It acts upon that for which it was composed with an act of overcoming and force, using numerical proportions and celestial secrets placed within specific bodies at favorable times, accompanied by strengthening incenses that attract the spirituality of that talisman. 

Its state is like that of the second "result," expressed as the **Elixir**, which transforms bodies into its own essence by overpowering them. It is a potent **ferment** <note>Arabic: *khamira*; a substance that initiates a transformation, like yeast in dough</note> that changes things from their very foundation. It is as dominant as a poison that spreads through the various types of bodies, transforming them into itself to change one person (or substance) into another through a power placed within it. Know, my brother, that the reality of the "ferment" or Elixir is a compound made of an earthy...

# Section (3)
### On the reality of the celestial sphere and its essence

<margin>6</margin> Know, O observer, that the celestial sphere is a solid body in the shape of a perfect globe, as are all the things within it in all their states and at all times. Some people have imagined that circumstances occur within the sphere that remove it from its circular shape at certain times, but it is not possible 
<margin>9</margin> for anything of that sort to happen at all. This is because the shape of the sphere is simply the shape of its Cause. <note>original: "علته" (illatihi) – Referring to the Neo-Platonic idea that the physical world mirrors the perfection of the spiritual "Cause" or Intellect.</note> This is because the Soul possesses this form—meaning it is the first "emitted" thing. This is because the First Thing, in which there is no corruption, has a perfect form, and the perfect form is the circle. 
<margin>12</margin> Likewise, it is formed from a single line because it is a First Cause. This is a matter whose proof is subtle. Furthermore, the sphere is an essence, while the "degrees" <note>The 360 degrees of the circle.</note> within it are merely a positional arrangement. When we begin with the positional degrees, we rise from them to 
<margin>15</margin> the necessary and obligatory matter. The path of instruction for this matter is the reverse. Furthermore, the teaching of the degrees is a path to teaching the conditions of the sphere, and it is not possible for anything...

<page-num>١٣</page-num>

...all beings. As for the actions of the <term>Degrees<note>original: "الدرج" (al-daraj) – The 360 individual degrees of the zodiac, each believed to have its own specific influence or "image."</note></term>, when a degree falls at any point whatsoever, and there is a fixed star within it, and then a **wandering star** <note>A planet.</note> reaches that point, you must recognize the effect of that planet on the earthly things in this world.

For example:
*   If **Saturn** moves things characterized by coldness and dryness;
*   **Jupiter** moves things characterized by heat and moisture;
*   **Mars** moves things characterized by heat and dryness;
*   **Venus** moves things characterized by weak heat and dominant moisture;
*   **Mercury** moves things characterized by weak heat and significant dryness;
*   And the **Moon** moves things characterized by coldness and moisture.

If the fixed stars are similarly disposed, and a degree is utilized by a planet that is purely hot but weak in its secondary qualities of dryness or moisture, and the **Sun** is alone in that place, you should judge that the matter will grow and increase. Likewise, if it happens that the planet is acting with its full power, the growth will be even greater. This is a difficult and highly <term>Obscure<note>original: "إغماض" (ighmad) – A term for the deliberate use of cryptic or coded language by ancient philosophers to protect secrets from the uninitiated.</note></term> topic among the early sages. For them, "obscurity" in speech meant to veil the literal meaning and hide the inner essence; this is what they called concealment. Know this well.

The bodies of the <term>World of Generation and Corruption<note>original: "عالم الكون والفساد" (alam al-kawn wa'l-fasad) – The Aristotelian term for the sublunary realm (Earth), where things are subject to birth, change, and decay.</note></term> are never found in the place of the <term>Sphere<note>original: "الفلك" (al-falak) – The celestial orbits or the heavens.</note></term>, nor is any part of the Sphere ever in the world of generation and corruption, unless by coercion. The Sphere, as we have said, is a rounded ball from all sides, possessing perfect circularity. A circle is formed from a single curved line, within which is a point where all lines drawn from it to the circumference are equal. That point is the center.

The reference to these "lines" is actually to the **casting of rays** <note>The astrological theory that planets emit beams of influence toward the Earth.</note> from the stars onto the world at the center. This is the secret behind the influence of **Talismans**; it is like a boundary or a design that has been agreed upon, since the Sphere is a globe encompassing the entire world, with neither a vacuum nor a plenum beyond it.

The <term>Ether<note>original: "الاثير" (al-athir) – The "fifth element" or quintessence that makes up the heavens, believed to be unchanging and eternal.</note></term> is a stationary form which serves as a dwelling. The sphere of the stars is within it, though it is deviated from its center, because its center is to the side of the center of the Earth, as has been said regarding the inclination. The nature of the Sphere is a single nature. The movement of bodies possessing natural qualities follows the movement of the Sphere. Its heat, which occurs accidentally, is what stirs the "becoming" within this world.

The degrees of the Sphere are 360 by the primary division. Likewise, there are 360 **Images** <note>Likely referring to the 360 "monomoiria" or individual images associated with each degree of the zodiac.</note>, and within them lies the "inner heart" of astrological judgments, for these judgments follow the geometric proportions.

Some people have disagreed, arguing that the Sphere itself has no utility; rather, they believe the utility comes from the **Ether** in the higher world, specifically through the stars and the heat. They claim the images within the degrees themselves are merely representations of the planetary positions when they are joined together. Another group says that the images of the degrees are the very essence of the science of the stars and the cause of all existence...

# Chapter (4)

### The Foundations of Talismanic Magic and the Mansions of the Moon

Furthermore, when people required the creation of a <term>Talisman<note>original: "الطلسم" (al-talsam) – An object inscribed with astrological symbols and created at a specific moment to capture the power of the heavens for a specific purpose.</note></term>, they found it necessary to understand the **Celestial Proportions** which form the very foundation of the craft. These proportions are what broadcast and manifest the effects of the talismans. I will provide you here with the principles of these celestial proportions, upon which you may build, serving as the astronomical blueprint for talismanic work.

The practitioner of talismans must be knowledgeable in astronomical calculations and <term>proportions<note>original: "النسب" (al-nisab) – The geometric and harmonic relationships between celestial bodies.</note></term>. Beyond this, they must be certain of the truth of their work, with no doubt or suspicion entering their mind. This certainty strengthens the action of the **Rational Soul**, allowing the practitioner’s will to connect with the "World Soul" <note>A Neoplatonic concept suggesting the universe itself has a soul that connects the physical and spiritual realms.</note> to achieve the desired result.

I must also inform you of a vital condition regarding the celestial realm closest to us: do not perform any work until the **Moon** is in the specific degree that corresponds to that work. The Moon has manifest effects that are not hidden, and I will detail its actions for you later. For now, I shall mention the effects of the Moon within the boundaries of its **Mansions**, specifically according to the consensus of the **Indian Sages** regarding the twenty-eight mansions.

(1) The first of these is **Al-Sharatan** <note>The "Two Signs," identified as the stars Beta and Gamma Arietis, marking the horns of the Ram (Aries).</note>. It spans from the beginning of Aries to twelve degrees, fifty-one minutes, and twenty-six seconds. The people of India say that when the Moon is in this mansion, it is auspicious for travel and for taking <term>laxative medicine<note>original: "الدواء المسهل" (al-dawa' al-mushil) – Medicines used to purge the humors, often timed with the moon's phases in medieval medicine.</note></term>. Make this a rule.

---

<margin>Notes on variants: 13 "from it" [omitted in some editions] | 13-14 [Hebrew characters in the Latin Picatrix version] | 13 "Indian Sages" | 14 "They use" or "He uses" [depending on the manuscript].</margin>

<column-break/>

For a traveler, you may construct a talisman in this mansion for his safety during his journey. Conversely, one may also construct a talisman in this mansion to sow discord between spouses or friends through separation and enmity. It is also used to create a talisman to cause a slave to flee or run away for whoever intends such a thing, and to ruin a partnership between associates because this mansion is of a <term>Malefic Fiery<note>original: "نحس نارى" (nahs nari) – Meaning it possesses the destructive or "burning" qualities associated with the element of fire and the planet Mars.</note></term> nature.

I will state a general rule for you here: in works of "good," always ensure the Moon is healthy and free from "combustion" <note>A planet is "combust" when it is too close to the Sun, which was believed to weaken its power or "burn" its influence.</note> or malefic influences. In works of "evil," let the Moon be combust and malefic; know this well.

(2) **Al-Butayn** <note>The "Little Belly," identified as stars in the constellation Aries (Delta, Epsilon, and Rho Arietis).</note>. It spans from twelve degrees, fifty-one minutes, and twenty-six seconds of Aries to the completion of twenty-five degrees, forty-two minutes, and fifty-two seconds of Aries. In this mansion, talismans are made for digging wells and rivers, for uncovering hidden requests and buried treasures, and for the growth of crops. One may also work talismans here to ruin a marriage before the couple can meet, as well as "exciting" talismans <note>Likely talismans for lust or intense attraction.</note> because it is of a **Benefic Fiery** nature. It is also used for causing a slave to flee and for strengthening the bonds of a prisoner if the intent is to cause them harm.

(3) **Al-Thurayya** <note>The Pleiades, a prominent star cluster in Taurus.</note>. It spans from twenty-five degrees, forty-two minutes, and fifty-two seconds of Aries to eight degrees, thirty-four minutes, and eighteen seconds of Taurus. In this mansion, a talisman is made for one who travels by sea, for he shall be saved. It is also suitable for talismans to ruin a partnership and for talismans to release prisoners from their bonds or to increase their punishment. In this mansion, one may also construct a talisman for success in the pursuit of **Alchemy** <note>original: "الكيمياء" (al-kimiya)</note> and the "service of fire," as well as talismans for land hunting and for fostering affection.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the twenty-eight Lunar Mansions, detailing Mansions 4 through 8. These mansions are used to time the creation of talismans for both benevolent purposes, such as trade and reconciliation, and malevolent ones, such as the destruction of cities or the separation of spouses. The text provides precise astronomical boundaries for each mansion in degrees, minutes, and seconds.</meta>

(6) ۞ **The Mansion of Al-Han'ah** <note>original: "الهنعة" (al-han‘ah) – Literally "the brand" or "the fold," often identified with stars in the constellation Gemini.</note> ۞ It extends from four degrees, seventeen minutes, and ten seconds of Gemini to seventeen degrees, eight minutes, and thirty-six seconds <margin>3</margin> of Gemini. Within it are crafted <term>talismans<note>original: "طلسمات" (talsamat) – Objects created under specific astrological alignments to influence earthly events.</note></term> for the destruction and siege of cities, seeking revenge against kings, and inflicting misfortune and evil upon enemies in every wretched state. It is also used for talismans to destroy crops, trusts, and deposits, as well as to improve the conditions of partners and land-based hunting. Additionally, it is used for a talisman to disrupt <margin>6</margin> the effectiveness of medicines when they are taken.

(7) ۞ **The Mansion of Al-Dhira‘** <note>original: "الذراع" (al-dhira‘) – "The Arm," referring to the extended arm of the Lion in ancient Arabic astronomy, located in Gemini.</note> ۞ It extends from seventeen degrees, eight minutes, and thirty-six seconds of Gemini to the end of Gemini. Within it is crafted a talisman for the growth and blessing of trade, <margin>9</margin> the growth of crops, and a talisman for the well-being and safety of travelers by water. It is also used to reconcile friends and partners. Within this mansion, one can "bind" flies so they do not enter a place. However, any industrial work performed during this time <margin>12</margin> will be ruined and require repeating a second time. It is also used for a talisman to achieve one's desires from a ruler or a person of high status one wishes to contact, a talisman for the return of a runaway slave, and a talisman to remove land, wealth, a house, or similar things from someone’s possession.

(8) ۞ **The Mansion of Al-Nathrah** <note>original: "النثرة" (al-nathrah) – "The Sneeze" or the "manger," corresponding to the stars in the constellation Cancer.</note> ۞ It extends from the beginning of Cancer to twelve degrees, fifty-one <margin>15</margin> minutes, and twenty-six seconds of Cancer. Within it are crafted talismans for love and friendship between those who hate one another, as well as talismans for the well-being of travelers and partners. Additionally, a talisman is made here to prolong the imprisonment of prisoners and captives, to ruin the condition of slaves, <margin>18</margin> and a talisman to drive away mice and bedbugs.

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the Lunar Mansions and the theoretical foundations of astrological magic. It transitions from the list of the twenty-eight mansions to the specific requirements for the practitioner, emphasizing the Indian origins of these methods and the philosophical concept of "readiness" (isti'dad) required for a talisman to take effect.</meta>

<page-num>٢٤</page-num>

These twenty-eight images are what the people of India rely upon in their endeavors and astrological selections; this is what we have found in the books of theirs that we have studied on this matter.

The primary principle in what we have presented is that the Moon, in whatever works of good you attempt, must be pure from the malefic planets <note>The "malefics" (nuhus) usually refer to Mars and Saturn, believed to exert a challenging or harmful influence.</note> and from "combustion" <note>A planet is "combust" when it is so close to the sun that its power is thought to be weakened or hidden.</note>, and it should be connecting with the benefics <note>The "benefics" (sa’ud) usually refer to Jupiter and Venus, associated with harmony and growth.</note>. At the beginning of your works, you should ensure it is moving away from a benefic and applying toward another benefic. In works of evil, the opposite is done—so know this.

As for our previous statement that the <term>maker of talismans</term> <note>original: "sāni’ al-tilsamāt"</note> needs to be precisely timed regarding the soundness of what he performs, this refers to the **readiness** of the practitioner. It is the preparation to receive the governed effects that are desired to occur. This kind of preparation exists only within the human character. As for the **readiness** in all other substances, it is the receptivity of natural substances—such as the readiness of wax to accept a form, or the receptivity of a possessed person to the possessor; for this is a readiness to accept the possession because their limbs are too weak to resist. You find this readiness in times of weakness alongside intensity. This type of readiness is required for the materials from which <term>talismans</term> are made, as not every material is capable of accepting just any random action. This is a fundamental principle agreed upon in their writings. When the readiness and preparation for reception are established, the reception itself must occur. When the reception occurs, **union** takes place, and the intended action appears. For union is the impression of accepting the form until the "hyle" <note>A philosophical term for "prime matter" or the raw substance of the universe.</note> and the form become one. This is like the adhering of a human's image in water or a mirror, or like the union of the Divine and the Human <note>original: "al-lahut fi al-nasut," referring to the dual nature of Christ in Christian theology</note> according to the Christians, or like the union of the soul with the body. Understand this and observe it clearly. Know that the intent behind composing these writings is nothing other than:

Returning to our purpose, I say: know that if your work is by day, you should place the Moon in the Ascendant, and let the Ascendant be one of the **diurnal** <term>zodiac signs</term>. If the Ascendant is one of the **straight-rising** <term>zodiac signs</term> <note>Signs that take longer to rise over the horizon in the northern hemisphere, associated with easier or more lasting success.</note>, it eases the work and carries it through. If the Ascendant is one of the **crooked-rising** <term>zodiac signs</term> <note>Signs that rise quickly or at an oblique angle, associated with difficulty or complication.</note>, it makes the work difficult—except that their soundness or corruption also depends on the aspect of the benefic or malefic planets toward them. If the Ascendant is straight-rising but a malefic planet looks upon it or is present within it, that will corrupt the work and make it difficult. If it is from the crooked <term>zodiac signs</term> but the benefics look upon it or are within it, they will make it easy. The same applies to nocturnal and diurnal <term>zodiac signs</term> if they rise out of their proper form—that is, if a diurnal sign rises at night or a nocturnal sign rises by day. If the benefics look upon them, they rectify them, but if the malefics look upon them, they increase the evil.

Therefore, the <term>maker</term> of the talisman has a necessary need to know the crooked, the straight, the fixed, the tropical <note>original: "al-munqaliba" (the turning or cardinal signs).</note>, the bicorporeal <note>Signs with "two bodies" like Gemini or Pisces, often called mutable signs.</note>, the diurnal, and the nocturnal signs. He must recognize the benefic and malefic planets, the purity of the Moon from the "accidents" that afflict it, and know which work of <term>talismans</term> each planet and each sign is suited for. He also has a dire need to watch for the lunar eclipse. Beware with all your effort of the lunar eclipse in works of charity, and of the Moon being "under the sun's rays" until it is released from the "node" <note>The points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note>. ### ->(17) ❊ Talisman for the Meeting and Affection of Two People ❊<-

<margin>6</margin> You shall fashion two talismans: one during the Ascendant of the specific question. Make the Ascendant and the Tenth House fortunate, and keep the malefics away from the Ascendant. Make the Lord of the Eleventh House <note>The house of friends and alliances</note> a benefic planet connected to the Lord of the Ascendant by a **trine** or **sextile** aspect <note>A 'trine' (120°) or 'sextile' (60°) are harmonious angles that allow for cooperation</note>, with mutual reception. I remind you here of what you must know: the reason why
<margin>9</margin> the sextile and trine aspects are viewed as indicators of love, agreement, and similarity is that the trine aspect connects a Fire sign to another Fire sign, Earth to Earth, Air to Air, and Water to Water. Therefore, it is the aspect of friendship and love. The sextile aspect connects Fire to Air, or Earth to Water; since they agree in their "active" qualities <note>Fire and Air are both active; Earth and Water are both passive</note> but differ in their "passive" ones, this became the aspect of friendship without the depth of love. The **square** aspect <note>A 90° angle</note> connects Water to Fire, or Air to Earth.
<margin>12</margin> Since they differ entirely in their nature, the square aspect became an indicator of distance and hatred due to the opposition of their natures. To return to our topic, I say: you shall fashion the second talisman—if it is for a friend—during the Ascendant of the Eleventh House. If it is for a husband or wife, fashion it during the Ascendant of the Seventh House. Ensure the significator of the Ascendant of the person you wish to win over is connected to the Lord of
<margin>14</margin> the first house, with mutual reception between them. Bury both talismans together in the location of the person seeking the affection; they shall then grow in harmony and never part.

### ->(20) ❊ Talisman for Affection and Submission ❊<-

Fashion two talismans during the Ascendant of Venus <note>When the sign rising on the horizon is ruled by Venus, or Venus herself is rising</note> in the first "face" <note>A 10-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign</note> of Cancer, while the Moon is in the first face of Taurus. Let Venus be in the Ascendant and the Moon in the Eleventh House <note>The house of friends and hopes</note>. Then, make the two images embrace and bury them in the location of one of the parties. This brings permanent love and intense affection. This proportion is known as the "Ratio of Exchange." **Ptolemy** alluded to this in his **"Book of the Fruit"** <note>The *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Claudius Ptolemy</note> in the thirty-third aphorism; look it up there, and I shall explain it further to you in the fourth discourse^a).

### ->(22) ❊ Talisman for Catching Fish ❊<-

Fashion the image of a fish in the likeness of whatever species of fish is found in that specific river. Do this when the Ascendant is in Pisces, with Jupiter located therein, and during the hour of Venus. First, fashion its head, then its body, then its tail. Assemble the parts at that same hour. Create a thin pillar of silver to hold the fish at its tip. Then, make a vessel of lead, place the pillar upright within it with the fish at the end, and fill the vessel with water. Seal the vessel, the water, and the talisman inside, closing the mouth of the vessel with a firm adhesive so that no water can escape. Cast the vessel into the bottom of that river, and the fish will gather from every direction toward that talisman.

### ->(23) ❊ Talisman for Banishing Scorpions ❊<-

Fashion the image of a scorpion out of gold while **the Moon is in** the Ascendant **or** in one of the "pivotal houses" <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses, which are points of greatest power</note> such as Taurus, Aquarius, or Leo. The best of these is Leo, because its nature is contrary to the nature of scorpions <note>Leo is a fire sign, scorpions are associated with the water sign Scorpio</note>. Let the Sun be in Leo, during the hour of the Sun, with Saturn in retrograde <note>Appearing to move backward, often used in magic for 'reversing' or 'undoing' things</note>. Fashion the tail first, then the two [back] legs, then the two [front] hands, and finally the head. Understand that this reversed order is for the purpose of "banishing" <note>To repel or negate</note>. When you have finished, attach the left hand and the left leg in the place of the right ones, and the right ones in the place of the left. Attach the head in its place, and likewise the tail. Fashion the stinger, then place the scorpion upside down on its back, with the stinger driven into its own back as if it has stung itself in the head. Then...

## (31) ❊ Talisman to repel melancholic diseases and establish health ❊
*For whomever you wish to heal, so that they attain the utmost quality and strength, and to repel the harm of illnesses.*

It should be performed during the last hour of Sunday, with the lord of the hour in the tenth house from the Ascendant. It should be made of pure silver, for this repels all that we have mentioned.

Among its conditions is that you must not perform any talismans for love or intimacy unless the Moon is with benefic planets during the <term>full days<note>The period of the waxing Moon leading up to the full moon, associated with growth and increase.</note></term>. Refers to when the Moon makes no further aspects to planets before changing signs.</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion of talismanic magic from the previous section, moving from the physical and astrological timing to the vital role of the "incantation" or spoken word. It emphasizes that the practitioner’s internal state and the specific phrasing used are what "breathe life" into the physical object.</meta>

All the masters of this craft have reached a consensus that the spoken word used in the construction of **talismans** for a specific purpose—accompanied by a plea for the effect to be accepted—is essential. Among them is the sage **"Timaeus"** <note>original: "Tyauws." Likely referring to Timaeus of Locri or a similar figure attributed in the Hermetic tradition; some manuscripts suggest "Thoos."</note> who said: "The speech used over talismans holds the same place as the soul does for the body; it is the mover of the spiritual powers." This is especially true if the speaker is focused and speaks with a sincere intention. That intention is the "noble element" through which all talismans are completed. The meaning of "speech" here is to speak words that agree with the intended outcome, according to the power the practitioner has prepared within his own soul and which flows through his mind.

**For example**, on talismans of **love and union**, one should say: 
"I have joined Person A and Person B just as fire, air, water, and earth are joined. I have moved the <term>spirituality<note>Original: "ruhaniyya." In medieval magic, this refers to the unseen, celestial essence or "spirit" of a planet or star that can be drawn down into an object.</note></term> of Person A just as the rays of the sun move the light of the world and its powers. I have beautified Person A in the eyes of Person B just as the sky is beautified by its stars and the plants by their flowers. I have made the spirituality of Person A rise above the spirituality of Person B just as fire rises above air, water, and earth. Person B shall not eat, nor drink, nor find pleasure or joy, except in the presence of Person A."

If you are crafting **enmity and separation**, say: 
"I have cut and separated Person A and Person B by the power of these spiritual beings, just as light is separated from darkness. I have placed enmity between them like the enmity between water and fire."

If you are crafting a **binding of lust** and its movements, say: 
"I have bound the spirituality of the lust of Person A from Person B (or from all women), and I have seized it by the power of these spiritual beings just as the mountains and their rocks are bound."

---
<note>Scholarly variants: The name "Timaeus" appears as "Thoos" in the Picatrix. Some manuscripts (S) read "intends" instead of "defines." Others (C) specify "Person B, daughter of Person B." Compare these passages to the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity, Volume IV.</note>

<column-break/>

When the spiritualities of the spheres are received through their placement and construction according to the true celestial proportions that match the desired goal, they become like **living bodies** that perform wondrous deeds.

**Aristotle** <note>In the Middle Ages, many magical and Neoplatonic texts were pseudepigraphically attributed to Aristotle to give them authority.</note> also said in one of his treatises: "The best thing upon which a talisman can be imprinted is the action of the **seven wandering stars** (the planets). The highest and most lasting of these is when a fortunate planet assists in bringing its spirituality down to the earth from the sphere." 

He further said: "There may be certain **Divine Names** which, if used to summon the spiritualities, cause them to descend and fall low. These names might even kill the one who summons them if he is not knowledgeable in the nature of the planetary spirituality being brought down."

This is similar to the references made by the masters of **Sufism** regarding the **Greatest Name** <note>The "Al-Ism al-A'zam," a hidden name of God in Islamic tradition believed to grant the user the power to perform miracles or change reality.</note>, which in their view transforms things from their natural state. Through the speaking of this Name, they produce marvelous effects in the world. However, the majority of the Sufis—meaning the common practitioners—hold beliefs contrary to this. I have written a specific treatise on this subject in which I gathered all of their sayings.

Returning to the words of **Aristotle**: He said regarding **magical incantations**—even though they do not leave the circle of the earth—that they are close to this art in the way they bring things down. However, incantations do not achieve their effect unless the practitioner's hope is tied to the **Supreme Deity**, for He is the one who moves the incantations, making them commanded and returning them to the <term>hyle<note>Original: "al-hayula." A term from Greek philosophy (hyle) referring to "prime matter" or the underlying substance of all physical things.</note></term>, directing them toward the center-point of the earth. This is the literal text of his words, and I will provide it to you in its entirety in the **Fourth Treatise** of this book of ours.

---
<note>Scholarly variants: Manuscript S omits "also." The sequences attributed to Aristotle are repeated in Book 4, page 327. Some versions (Picatrix) use the word "center" instead of "point of the earth." The reference to the "Fourth Treatise" was supplied in the margin of manuscript C.</note>

This is self-evident to the mind of anyone who reflects upon it, and it is a matter already concluded. However, you should know that our reference in "The Rank" <note>Original: "al-Rutba." ## Section (6)

<margin>6</margin> Know, may God honor you, that wisdom is very noble, and attaining it is an honor and a splendor. Wisdom consists of levels, some of which serve as a ladder to others. The perfect human is the one who encompasses the fruits of wisdom by acquiring it, for he is the one who loves its acquisition. They defined <term>Philosophy<note>Original: "Falsafa," derived from the Greek *philosophia* (love of wisdom).</note></term> rightly when they gave it various definitions, the most noble of which is that it is <margin>9</margin> the preference for wisdom. Whoever falls short of this rank is not truly counted as a human, even if he is human in form, for he does not look into the reality of his own existence—that he is a <term>Microcosm<note>Original: "al-'alam al-saghir," literally "the small world." A central medieval concept suggesting the human body and soul mirror the structure of the entire universe.</note></term> corresponding to the <term>Macrocosm<note>Original: "al-'alam al-kabir," literally "the great world" or the universe.</note></term>. His reality is that he is a complete part possessing a rational, vegetative, and animal soul. He is unique in possessing all three, whereas other animals lack <margin>12</margin> the <term>Rational Soul<note>Original: "al-Nafsi al-Natiqa." In medieval philosophy, "rational" (natiqa) also implies the faculty of speech and logical discourse.</note></term>. The meaning of "rational" here is the "discerning" faculty, because it is the power that causes the development of crafts, brings the absent to mind through thought, composes images, and envisions what has not been seen. It brings existing things and distant lands into the mind and links what is heard to its own powers and essence. Through it, a person sees in his sleep what will happen in his day. Thus, he is the Microcosm <margin>15</margin> contained within the Macrocosm, harmonizing with it because his form is connected to its forms, and all things within the universe are present within him.

<column-break/>

<page-num>٤٣</page-num>

He shares traits with all animals but differs from them through sciences and clever stratagems. He possesses six directions of movement; the bones of his spine and thighs move in a straight line. He dies by nature but lives by accident <note>This refers to the philosophical distinction between natural death (the breakdown of the body) and accidental life (the soul's temporary attachment to the body).</note>. <margin>3</margin> He has fingers and palms, a rounded head, nails, and a distinctive gait. He is capable of receiving sciences and writing, and is an inventor of crafts. He mimics animals, but they do not mimic him. He is a laughing and crying creature, using crying as an expression of grief. Within him is a divine power and a capacity for civic governance. He is like a statue, but his interior is light; his body <margin>6</margin> is his statue, and his soul is its inhabitant. He is upright in form, capable of distinguishing what harms him from what benefits him. He acts with intention when he plans, moves with purpose, and exercises theoretical and intellectual restraint. He invents delicate crafts and wonderful, miraculous <term>Talismans<note>Original: "al-Tilsamat." Objects inscribed with astrological signs or incantations believed to exert supernatural influence.</note></term>. He preserves the forms of sciences and transcends all physical sensations. <margin>9</margin> God has made him the treasurer of His wisdom, the interpreter of His own self and of all His creations, the recipient of His revelation, the vessel of His sciences, and the one who delivers His message. He is the offspring of the Macrocosm and its copy, gathering its meanings within his own creation and composition. While other creatures are scattered, he unites them, but they do not unite him. He subjects them <margin>11</margin> to his will, but they do not subject him. He mimics their sounds and represents their forms with his hand, describes them with his tongue, and reports on their natures. No other animal is able to change or depart from its natural creation, nor can it mimic the voice of another; thus, the rooster does not go beyond its crowing, nor the dog its barking, nor the lion its roaring. Yet man, <margin>15</margin> despite this, can change his voice and his character, manifesting as whatever he wishes and governing himself and others. He is the possessor of a dense body and a subtle spirit; part of him is subtle and part is dense. Part of him is subtle and living, and part is dense and dead. Half of him is motion and half is stillness. Half of him is engraved and half <margin>18</margin> is blank. Half of him is night and half is day. Half of him is darkness and half is light. Half of him is manifest and half is hidden.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the human being as a Microcosm (a "small world"). Having established the definition of philosophy on the previous page, the author now provides a detailed anatomical and cosmological correspondence, mapping the human body's structures to the earth, the stars, and the mechanisms of a kingdom.</meta>

<page-num>45</page-num>

...the flesh of his body is like the earth, his bones like mountains, his hair like plants, his veins like valleys, and <margin>3</margin> his internal organs like minerals.

His body is composed of nine substances built upon nine circles, one inside the other, with the encompassing sphere surrounding them. These are: flesh, bones, muscle, nerve, marrow, <margin>6</margin> skin, hair, and nails. Thus, the marrow is inside the bones, and its function is to preserve strength and to soften the dryness of the bones. The function of the bones is to hold the flesh and provide it stability. The function of the muscles is to bind the joints <margin>9</margin> and move the limbs. The function of the flesh is to fill the gaps of the body and protect the bones so they do not separate or break. The function of the veins is to collect blood and facilitate its flow to the extremities of the body. The function of the <margin>12</margin> blood is to hold heat, regulate life, balance the temperament <note>Original: "mizaj," the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) determining health and personality.</note>, and generate movement. The function of the skin is to encompass the entire body and its contents like a wall around it. The function of the nails is to support the tips of the limbs, <margin>15</margin> clutching and binding them so they do not fray or break.

Within the structure of the body are twelve openings <note>Original: "thuqban," referring to the orifices.</note>, corresponding to the twelve signs of the Zodiac. Just as six of the signs are southern and six are northern, there are six openings on the <margin>18</margin> left side of a human and six on the right side, corresponding exactly in quantity and quality. Furthermore, just as there are seven wandering planets in the heavens by which the decrees of the spheres and all created things are governed—and through which the order of all existences is maintained—so too are there seven active forces in the human body, emanating from the human soul, through which the well-being of the body is achieved. Since these planets possess souls, bodies, actions, and spiritualities <note>Original: "ruhaniyyat," the celestial spiritual influences or "intelligences" associated with planets in medieval Neoplatonism.</note> that act upon the manifest world of minerals, animals, and plants, there are likewise found in the human body physical forces that act upon the body to ensure its survival and well-being through the materials of seven other psychic powers: the Retentive, the Attractive, the Digestive, the Expulsive, and the Nutritive <note>The text lists five here, though it references seven; these were the standard "natural faculties" in medieval medicine.</note>.

...inner [being], half of which is perceived by the senses and half by the intellect; half is the carrier and half the carried. He feels shame at <margin>3</margin> what is foul, endures, acts as he wishes, and feels regret. He is composed of both subtle and gross substances: he contains the density of Earth, the subtlety of Air, the thinness of Fire, and the coldness of Water. Therefore, he has become <margin>6</margin> balanced through movement, which is the spirit of life. He recognizes the heat of fire through the potential fire within him, and he recognizes the coldness of water through the coldness within him, and likewise for the other elements <term>Elements<note>Original: "ustuqussat," from the Greek *stoicheia*, referring to the four fundamental building blocks: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note></term>.

Furthermore, his head is like the celestial sphere in its form, its roundness, and the gathering of subtle <margin>9</margin> lights within it: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and speech. His two eyes are like the two luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>, his nostrils are like the two winds, and his ears are like the East and the West. His front is like the day, his back is like the night, his walking is like the movement of the stars, <margin>12</margin> his sitting is like their stationary positions, his retreating is like their descent, and his death is like their combustion.

His internal organs are seven, like the seven wandering planets. In his head are seven bones, as the <margin>15</margin> number of the seven days. In his back are twenty-four vertebrae, following the number of the hours of the day and night. He has twenty-eight joints, following the number of the lunar mansions and the letters of the alphabet. In his belly, the intestines correspond to the number of days of the crescent moons. He contains three hundred and sixty pulsing veins <note>Arteries.</note> and an equal number of still veins <note>Veins.</note>, corresponding to the <margin>18</margin> days and nights of the year and the degrees of the celestial sphere. He contains temperaments equal to the number of the seasons of the year.

Thus, his eyes are the spies of the Rational Faculty—which is like the King—and his ears are his informants. The tongue is his translator, the heart is the registry of his knowledge, the stomach is his treasury and the pot of the body. The liver is his steward <note>Reading "sammuhu" as "his steward" or "storer."</note>, and the gallbladder is his patience <note>Or "bitterness."</note> so that his flesh does not putrefy; it is the salt of the body and its medicine. The lungs are his fan, the hands are his chamberlains, and the feet are his mount.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the human being as a microcosm. Having previously linked the body’s faculties to the planets and celestial spheres, the text now moves into a deeper metaphysical discussion of the "Universal Man" versus the "Physical Man," and the nature of the four elements—fire, water, air, and earth—as they exist in their pure state versus their physical manifestations.</meta>

<margin>1</margin> Fire, when it is in a place other than its own in our world, is there by accident <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the essential nature of a thing, like the heat of water or the location of a flame</note>. When it leaves the body or the wood, it returns to its origin and its proper place above the air. As for its simple, universal action, it is beyond description and beyond <margin>3</margin> what can be grasped by words or spoken by a tongue, for it is a magnificent, supreme power. It is above simplicity and above quality, as are all the other elements <term>Astuqissat: the four fundamental elements (earth, water, air, fire) from the Greek "stoicheia"</term>.

The human being follows this same path. This is the Human who took the covenant in pre-eternity <note>A reference to the "Day of Alast," a Quranic concept where all human souls testified to God's Lordship before the creation of the world</note>, <margin>6</margin> and around whom the "composite" human revolves. It is only the human's mixing and blending with the various things that later attach to him—as accidents in different states and locations that he cannot escape—that has changed his form. These additions have altered him and made him share traits with animals, plants, and the elements; therefore, he became <margin>9</margin> similar to all things. When a person recognizes this truth and follows the path of spiritual discipline <note>Original: "tadbir," referring to the management of the self or soul</note> that leads him back to the lights of the First Principle—which is his own specific, essential order and his origin—he becomes more complete in his humanity than others, in proportion to his liberation. All of this is achieved by practicing the virtues according to his capacity. Therefore, <margin>12</margin> this [physical being] is the "partial" human: sensory, corporeal, thick-bodied, and a composite of a partial soul, a partial intellect, and a body. It is the shared, vanishing form which, in this lower world, is merely an idol <note>Original: "sanam," used here to mean a physical representation or statue</note> and a shell for that Universal, Intellectual, Spiritual Human—the noble, subtle, <margin>15</margin> simple, and primordial being <note>Original: "hayulani," referring to "materia prima" or the fundamental potentiality of being</note>. This latter is the pure form that does not reside in a body and remains forever in that higher world.

The form of the Universal Man is hidden within the form of the Partial Man, serving as its simple essence and its primary matter. The form of the Partial Man is hidden within the physical body and is its simple essence. The form of the body is a <margin>18</margin> composite idol and a shell for the form of the Partial Man, and the form of the Partial Man is a composite idol and a shell for the [Universal Man].

<column-break/>

...by the senses. However, the intelligible aspect of it is one, never shifting in its essence nor changing. Any change that occurs to it is directed toward sensory perfection.

<margin>3</margin> Let me provide you an example to help you understand this meaning, for it is an unusual way of speaking. One example is that the individual elements <note>Astuqissat</note> only became "elements" because of the way each was arranged in its place and the <margin>6</margin> accidental qualities that entered into them in their specific ranks. Water only acquired this wet, cold nature because of its location and the attachments that joined it in the order of creation. As for its first existence, which preceded its status as an "element," it remains in its universality. These universals exist in themselves whether or not a human perceives them or <margin>9</margin> understands them, for existence is essential to them.

The same applies to the Universal Man: existence is essential to him. The proof of the truth of what I have told you is that there is fire within water and water within fire, and that the elements are intertwined, <margin>12</margin> acting upon one another. Were it not for this, nothing would exist.

Likewise, human wills and desires are connected to the First Wills and Desires, and the effects of the cosmos flow through them, even if this is not apparent to the "partial" <note>individual</note> human. For although <margin>15</margin> this human's will and desire may not be effective in all of his states and actions, they are effective in some. Their effectiveness in the whole is not apparent to him unless he is one of those who has training and experience in the theoretical sciences; to such a person, this becomes clear.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the human being as a microcosm. Having previously linked the body’s faculties to the planets and celestial spheres, the text now moves into a deeper metaphysical discussion of the "Universal Man" versus the "Physical Man," and the nature of the four elements—fire, water, air, and earth—as they exist in their pure state versus their physical manifestations.</meta>

The Universal Human and the image of the Universal Human are but a likeness and a shell for the image of the Universal Soul. The Universal Soul, in turn, is a likeness and a shell for the Universal Intellect, and the Universal Intellect is a likeness and a shell for the Light from which the Intellect was originated <note>original: "ibda'" — a term in Islamic philosophy referring to the creation of something from nothing, without prior matter or time</note>. This Light serves as the primary matter <term>Hyle: from the Greek "hyle," referring to the fundamental, formless "stuff" that underlies all physical reality</term> for the Universal Intellect. Likewise, for everything below it: the higher is always the matter for that which is beneath it, being "simple" in relation to it. Conversely, that which is below is always the "form" of that which is above it, being "composite" in relation to it. The true Human is the composite form of the soul which makes use of the physical bodies joined by nature.

Whoever wishes to know this truth should be virtuous and pure of mind and body from defilement, for then he shall see and witness it with a true vision.

By these words—may God aid you with His help, O seeker—we have not strayed from our intended purpose. Rather, this is the very goal of writing this book, as it is the foundation for the science of talismans. If you are practiced in the sciences, you will verify this and recognize it as manifest magic <note>original: "al-sihr al-mubin"</note>. It was upon this principle that Plato <note>original: "Aflaton"</note>, the man brilliant in the sciences and foremost in virtue, built his book called *Timaeus*. He spoke at great length regarding "Forms," making this intention clear, yet he veiled his speech and imbued it with obscurity, as is the habit of the Sages to protect their wisdom from the ignorant. Proclus <note>original: "Barqalis" — a reference to the Neoplatonist philosopher Proclus Lycaeus</note> did the same.

Obscurity in the sciences, for them, refers to the subtlety of meanings, such that they become hidden and faint. Thus, the one who wishes to extract that hidden meaning requires thought, reflection, and refinement to distinguish it from the obvious, external matters with which it is mixed. For the sciences are of two types: the manifest and external, and the hidden and internal. The hidden and internal is what is "obscure," and that obscure meaning may require analogy and premises...

<column-break/>

...which then produce that obscure result, or it may require observation, deduction, and deep thought until that meaning dawns upon him and the intention is explained, and what was closed to him opens, allowing him to grasp his objective. Deduction is achieved through many means, including comparing the seen to the unseen, or tracing a "branch" back to its "root" via a common meaning, or basing one's view on accepted sayings from a respected individual or group, from which a conclusion is drawn, revealing the sought-after meaning. In short, once a path to knowledge is established, the seeker directs his gaze along that path, obtaining through this observation the meanings of all existing things and discerning their levels of hierarchy.

## Chapter (7)

Know—may God honor you—that existing things have distinct ranks. The existence of the Creator—Exalted is He—is the most excellent of existences, the most noble, and the most perfect in rank. Following Him in the rank of existence is the Intellect. From the Intellect comes the existence of the Soul, and after it, Primary Matter <term>Hyle: the formless substrate of reality</term>. All of these are stationary and cannot be described by local motion <note>Meaning they do not move from one physical place to another, as they are spiritual/metaphysical entities</note>. After these comes the Sphere of Nature, which is the beginning of motion and rest; from it begins "generation and corruption" <term>The cycle of birth, decay, and death in the physical world</term> in this world. After the Sphere of Nature come the celestial spheres down to the Sphere of the Moon. Below the Moon, there exists a "common matter" which has a sensory rank; this means that things exist within it in potentiality, not yet in actuality. Following this are the Elements <term>Astuqissat: the four fundamental elements (earth, water, air, fire) from the Greek "stoicheia"</term> that operate within that common matter, for the elements only act upon matter. After the elements come minerals, then plants, and then animals.

It concludes by outlining the ranks of existence, from the Creator down to minerals, plants, and animals.</summary>

solitary substance before its quality. "Matter" is the gathering of these simple elements to receive "Form." "Matter" is more general 
<margin>15</margin>than "Form" because Matter is "simple" <note>original: "sadaj" — meaning plain or unformed</note> before it accepts shaping. Once it accepts shaping, it becomes 
a "Form," just as the matter of copper is for the form of the jug, or the matter of wood is for the form of the chair. Once it accepts 
motion, rest, and the power mixed within it, it becomes a "Nature." Once the natures are gathered and accept 
<margin>18</margin>color, growth, or division, they become a "Body." The "Body" is either growing or non-growing. The "Growing Thing" is either animal or non-animal.

## Chapter One

<margin>6</margin> May God honor you. The aspirations of those with universal intellects have never ceased to strive toward knowing the secrets of the sages. They seek that which the sages hid in their books through symbols and riddles <note>original: "al-ramz wa-l-lughz"</note> regarding wondrous matters. Such seekers eventually achieved their desire and goal. But how can those with deficient intellects reach their aims? May God not deprive us or you, and may He illuminate our minds.
<margin>9</margin> Among the motivations that moved me to research the secrets of talismans <note>The word "talisman" comes from the Arabic "tilasm," which in turn comes from the Greek "telesma," meaning a completed rite or consecrated object.</note> is that in the bloom of my youth, I saw the virtuous Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 CE), the Greco-Egyptian astronomer whose works formed the basis of medieval science.</note> saying in his famous book *The Fruit*: "The images in the world of composition are submissive to celestial images." <note>original: "Kitab al-Thamara," known in Latin as the "Centiloquium." It is a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note> 
<margin>12</margin> The words of the sages testify by consensus that the stars possess powers according to their natural habits. Therefore, the masters of talismans drew these images when the stars occupied them, aiming to achieve specific works. They reached their goals through the excellence of their insight into the composition of—

So I made one myself and began stamping frankincense with it for those who were stung. I would change the material I stamped on, fearing 
<margin>12</margin> that the effect might be due specifically to the properties of the frankincense. I saw from this the most wonderful of wonders. Here his words ended.

Perception is the soul’s awareness, and its definition can only be established after knowing what
<margin>6</margin> "sense" is. Sensation is the change in the temperament of the sense-organs' qualities through direct contact with sensible things. Perception is the awareness of those sensing faculties regarding the change in the temperaments of the senses. For example, the visual power
<margin>9</margin> travels through the eye, and it is hidden within the pupils in the ocular organ made of crystalline humor <note>original: "al-rutuba al-jalidiyya."
