In our prayer, and to Him we are sincere in our devotions; through our worship of Him, we draw near to Him with our intention. He is our pillar, our preparation, our God, our treasure, our object of worship, our Creator, our Originator, our Quickener, and the ultimate end of our hope. To Him we lean our backs, and to His name we have surrendered our names; thus His name has become a shield for us, a sanctuary for us from our enemies, and a protection for us from all who plot against our purpose.

And [it is also] for His servant, the Moon—the King who is obedient to Him, who magnifies His power, prostrates before Him, and is diligent in His service—who refers its light back to Him and is granted its strength by Him. The Moon is eternal in His kingdom and His guidance, submissive to His greatness, rushing toward His obedience, and standing in awe within it forever and always, without flagging for the blink of an eye or falling short for a single moment. Upon them both <note>Likely referring to the deity and the Moon.</note> be prayer and praise from us for ever and ever, and for all ages. Amen, Amen.

Abu Bakr ibn Wahshiyya mentioned in the "Nabataean Agriculture" <note>A 10th-century Arabic work claiming to translate ancient Babylonian/Nabataean knowledge on farming and magic.</note> a prayer for Saturn <note>original: *Zuhal*</note>, noting that they say: "Beware the evil of this god when he is descending, or setting away from the Sun, or hidden by its rays, or in the midst of his retrograde motion <note>The apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky, often considered an ill omen in ancient astrology.</note>." 

So, offer to him this prayer that I mention, and burn incense for his idol using old hides, fat, filth, and a dead bat. Burn for him fourteen dead bats and the same number of mice; take their ashes and prostrate upon them before his idol. Prostrate to him upon a black rock or black sand, and seek refuge through that from his evil, for he is the cause of the destruction of everything that perishes, the affliction of everything that withers, and the weeping of every weeper. He is the lord of all poverty, hardship, imprisonment, grief, stinginess, and misery when he is angry. But when he is pleased, he grants endurance, long life, high reputation, status, and wealth, and he bestows these as an inheritance upon children and descendants.

And he makes that <note>the favor</note> endure in the descendants of the one given [the blessing]. His pleasure occurs during the oriental rising <note>When a planet rises in the east just before the sun.</note>, in the midst of his direct motion, in the speed of his travel and ascent, and when he is at his apogee <note>The point in a planet's orbit where it is furthest from the Earth.</note>.

> Magnification from us, and glorification, prayer, and worship. We stand upon our feet, upright for our Living and Eternal God, who never ceases and will never cease; the One who is unique in Lordship over all things; He who is **Z H L** <note>The Hebrew letters Zayin, Het, Lamed (ז ח ל), spelling "Zuhal" or Saturn.</note>, eternal in His heaven, effective in His power, solitary in His might, pride, and greatness; encompassing all and capable over all. The earth was moved despite its permanence like the weight of His movement. If He willed, He could have made everything other than it is, but He is Wise, acting by the power of wisdom, Knowing, with knowledge penetrating all. Blessed are You, Lord of the Heaven and other things, and sanctified and pure are Your noble names.

...[by Your] Beautiful [Names], we worship You and pray to Your eternity. We ask You by Your names, Your eternity, and Your generosity to keep our minds firm on their path as long as we are alive, and to be gentle with our bodies after departing life in <margin>3</margin> the trial <note>Likely referring to the "Trial of the Grave" in Islamic/Near Eastern eschatology.</note>. Drive the worms away from our flesh, for You are a Merciful, Eternal Lord. There is no mercy for Your harshness, and You are forceful, never regretting, far-reaching in power, and slow to act <note>A reference to God's patience; He does not rush to punishment.</note>. You are the Lord; whoever You give to, no one can prevent, and no one can give if You prevent.
<margin>6</margin> You are the Lord, unique in Lordship, solitary in Your authority, Lord of the stars and the planets circling in their orbits. They tremble at the sound of Your movement and are terrified by Your awe. We ask You to keep us safe from Your wrath, to push away Your power from us, and to have mercy on us from Your great evil <note>In the context of planetary worship, "evil" often refers to the destructive astrological influence of a planet like Saturn if not properly propitiated.</note>. O God, we ask You <margin>9</margin> to ward off Your strikes from us by Your Beautiful Names, through which whoever seeks Your mercy will find it. So have mercy on us, then grant us satisfaction through Your power and Your names, and by Your High, Sublime, and Great Name, we ask You to have mercy on us.

<margin>12</margin> This is the text of the words of "Ibn Wahshiyya" from the Nabataeans, translated in "The Agriculture." We have only mentioned this because of the consensus of these ancient generations on the worship of the stars and adopting their natures. These matters were permissible to them in their religions and laws. As for our community <margin>15</margin> and our Law <note>Islamic Sharia.</note>, using them is disbelief <term>disbelief: *kufr*, indicating practices that place a person outside the faith</term>. Therefore, the execution of the sorcerer was commanded in our community for using what we have mentioned and for rebelling against the commands of our faith. We only mentioned what we did so as not to omit any variety of these results which we are in the process of uncovering; they are also historical accounts.

another, then you say while you are alone these words: **Dahamus**, **Armas**, **Hilis**, **Maghas**, **Idris**, **Tamis**, **Farus**, **Dahidas**, **Afrawus**, **Kay'aqiras**. As for the call of the spirituality of **Mars** <note>original: *al-Marrikh*</note>: set out on Tuesday when the Sun has entered Aries <note>the zodiac sign where Mars is traditionally dignified</note>—which is the house of Mars—and the Moon is in the mansion of *Sa'd al-Bul'a* <note>The "Luck of the Swallower," the 23rd lunar mansion</note>, the exaltation of Mars. Place a large table in a corner of the house upon a sturdy low stand. Place a censer made of the planet's corresponding metal <note>tin, for Jupiter</note> before you. Place upon the table first: musk, camphor, agarwood, the "triple-scent" <note>original: *al-muthallatha*, a compound perfume</note>, civet, and a handful of mastic. Then arrange the cakes in their proper order and place the moist and dry sweets upon that table. In the center, place a lit candle, and beside it four open baskets filled with thin bread, cold roasted meat, and cooked meat from lambs, chickens, and young birds, along with various greens. Beside each basket, place a jug full of wine, a clean cup, and fragrant basil arranged between them. Then fumigate with agarwood at the table and with mastic in a corner of the room.

When these are cast upon it, it will melt and its harmful qualities will vanish. After mixing it thoroughly, place it in a small pot coated with the **Clay of Wisdom** <note>original: *tin al-hikma*, a specialized sealant used by alchemists to ensure airtight heating</note> and place it over the glow of embers. <margin>6</margin> Blow upon it gently until it melts like wax. When it reaches this state, remove it from the fire and let it cool. This "body," O King, is the aid for every **talisman** <note>original: *nayranj*, a term for sorcery or the production of wondrous effects</note> and enchantment.

Then he mentioned a bead called the <note>original: *al-Amâtîs*</note> **Amethyst Bead**. Its function, through talismanic art, is for rain, hail, and the snow that might afflict a king and his army on the march. He should raise it on his palm toward the heavens, and it will repel <margin>9</margin> these things from him; no harm shall befall him, his companions, or his beasts. This bead is dust-colored. Its making requires that you take two mithqals of iron and melt it with white **frankincense** <note>original: *al-kundur*</note>. Once melted, add one mithqal of silver and one mithqal of lead. When <margin>12</margin> they have mixed, set the mixture aside and combine it with "spiritual souls." This is done by taking the bones of the hands and feet of a pig, cleaning them of flesh and sinew, and cooking them in water and salt. Then dry them, crush them, and melt them with **mandrake** <note>original: *al-yabrûh*</note>. Place equal layers in a coated jug: a layer of mandrake, <margin>15</margin> a layer of **potash** <note>original: *qali*</note>, and a layer of bones until the jug is full. Place it in a fire of burning dung for one night. It will melt within; then take it out, let it cool, grind it, and cast some red arsenic upon it.

## Chapter (10)

<margin>3</margin> He mentioned in the book *The Istimâkhis* <note>original: *al-Istimâkhis*, possibly referring to the *Stomachos* or a similar mechanical/mathematical work repurposed as magic</note>, which he composed for Alexander, four beads in which he employed the craft of **talismans** and what is required by **spiritual science**. One <margin>6</margin> is called the **Damatîs Bead**. He commanded him to set it as a stone in his signet ring. Then, no human nor any spirit shall look upon him without being humbled in obedience and submission, accepting his command. If you seal a letter with it and it reaches a king or anyone else, his limbs will tremble <margin>8</margin> when he looks at it, and your commands and prohibitions shall be carried out. If you use the seal against a rebellious demon, he will submit to you and be humbled. This is its manufacture: it is red. Take one mithqal of red ruby, grind it, and add one **danig** <note>a small unit of weight, 1/6th of a dirham</note> of diamond ground with lead, two danigs of magnesia, <margin>12</margin> two danigs of sulfur, and one mithqal of gold. Gather all of this in a **crucible** <note>original: *bûtaqa*</note> and blow upon it gently until it all melts and flows. For the diamond melts the ruby, the magnesia melts the diamond, the sulfur melts the magnesia, and the gold melts the entire mixture. When it has all melted and flows <margin>15</margin> like water, remove the crucible and leave it to cool. Then extract from it a substance <note>original: *jawhar*</note> which you will find to be of a murky, mixed color. Set it aside. Then take the brain of a lion, the fat of a leopard, and the blood of a hyena, one equal part of each. Melt the fat and mix it with the brain, then pour <margin>18</margin> the blood over them; its color will become dusty-grey. Beware of touching it with your hand or letting it touch your clothes. Be cautious...

...Musk weighing a **daniq** <note>a small unit of weight, roughly 0.5 grams</note>, and of feverfew, seedless raisins, and white sandalwood, half a **mithqal** <note>approx. 2.12 grams</note> of each. Combine these, grind them into a fine powder, and knead them with the juice of crushed **myrtle** <note>original: *al-âs*</note>. Form them into pellets <term>shiyaf<gloss>traditionally eye-salves or suppositories, here used as protective plugs</gloss></term> and let them dry. When the practitioner intends to work with these compound poisons, he should dissolve a pellet and place it in his nostrils and his ears, and hold a pellet in his mouth. Furthermore, he must wear a veil over his face <note>original: *yatalaththamu*, referring to the *litham* or mouth-veil</note> while grinding and mixing them.
When handling them with his hands, he requires another compound to prevent them from harming his skin. He should take laurel berries, **mahaleb** <note>the seeds of the St. Lucie cherry</note>, and gentian—one part of each—and four parts each of balsam oil and rabbit blood. Grind the dry ingredients well, knead them with the balsam oil and rabbit blood, and store the mixture in a glass bottle. When he wishes to touch any of those [poisonous] substances, he must thoroughly coat his hands with this oil. Then he may handle those compounds and poisons, for they will neither injure nor harm him.

It was also mentioned in the **Book of the Asnutas** <note>original: *Kitâb al-Asnûtâs*; likely a corrupted Greek title, possibly related to Hermetic or astrological texts</note> that if the spiritual essence <term>ruhaniyya<gloss>the celestial or supernatural power associated with an object or ritual</gloss></term> of the **Niranjat** <note>original: *al-Nîranjât*; a term for magical arts, talismans, or deceptive illusions</note> turns against its maker, harming or sickening him according to the friction it causes with the natural humors that generate disease, then this compound should be administered as a drink: Take half an **uqiya** <note>an ounce</note> of human blood and dissolve it with two **mithqals** of almond oil. Take two **mithqals** of rabbit brain and mix it into one **uqiya** of donkey urine. Mix these well and have the patient drink two **dirhams** <note>approx. 6.24 grams</note> weight of it for seven consecutive days. It must be swallowed <note>original: *sahhan*, meaning to pour or swallow quickly</note> on an empty stomach. This will purge everything that has mixed with his corrupted nature and dissolve the spiritual influence of the **Niranjat**, regardless of which category of the **Seven Stars** <note>the seven classical planets: Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note> it belongs to.

...And all of that comes out, its spiritual essence <term>ruhaniyya<gloss>spiritual force</gloss></term> is balanced, its corrupted nature is rectified, and it becomes good and excellent.
It was mentioned in a book of his called *The Malatis* <note>original: "al-Malatis"; likely a corruption of a Greek title</note> that when Alexander asked Kinas, the Indian sage and maker of talismans, whether he had written a book on the subject, he replied, "Yes." He then produced this book called *The Malatis*, in which he mentions the talismans that Kinas created in his writings. This man, Kinas, was known as "The Spiritualist." He lived for five hundred and forty years and was present during the time of Hadrian <note>original: "Adriyânûs"</note>, the tyrannical and murderous king. Kinas crafted talismans composed between the Macrocosm <note>the universe</note> and the Microcosm <note>the human being</note> using speech composed of the spiritualities spread throughout the world. Through this, he would win over the heart of this king and all other kings. He likewise crafted talismans for other purposes. 

Among these is the preparation of the talisman called **Daghitus**, which he made for the union of men and women. Its preparation is as follows: take half a **daniq** <note>a small weight, about 0.5 grams</note> of deer brain, half a **daniq** of melted sheep-tail fat, a **daniq's** weight of camphor, and half a **daniq's** weight of rabbit brain. Gather the brains in a vessel for nasal medicine <note>original: "mus'at"</note> and place it over hot coals until it melts. Then, cast the sheep-tail fat upon it until it melts, then cast the crushed camphor. Next, remove it and fashion a hollow figurine out of unused wax. Set your intention upon the woman you wish to draw and incline toward you. Then, pierce a hole from its mouth leading into its hollow interior and pour that mixture into its belly. While you are doing this, say: Dehyayis, Ghanamwadis, Taq'ayis, Dirolayis. Then, take the weight of one **mithqal** of white **Tabarzad** sugar <note>a high-quality, hard crystalline sugar</note> and place it in its mouth. Take a thin silver nail and drive it into its chest (without it passing through to the other side), and at that moment say: Hadoras, Tamaros.

<vocab>
**Nayranj**: (Arabic: نيرنج) A category of magic involving the use of natural substances to produce supernatural effects.
**Kunder**: (Arabic: الكندر) Frankincense, used here for ritual purification and as a carrier for the spell.
**Kayya**: (Arabic: الكية) A substance used in incense, possibly a resin or caustic mineral.
**Mithqal**: (Arabic: مثقال) A unit of weight equal to about 4.25 grams.
**Sha'ira**: (Arabic: شعيرة) Literally "a grain of barley," a tiny unit of weight.
</vocab>

# Description of a magic trick <note>original: *nayranj*</note> called Baghis, used to turn the hearts of kings toward their subjects
It is used to gain their love and incline them toward kindness and gentleness. Its preparation is to take wax that has never been used for <margin>3</margin> anything and fashion it into a hollow statue in the name of the King you desire. Then take one **danq** of a doe’s brain, two **danqs** of a rabbit’s brain, and one **mithqal** of human blood. Gather all of this in a vessel <note>original: *mas'at*</note> and add to the mixture half a **mithqal** <margin>6</margin> of powdered camphor, two **danqs** of ambergris, and half a **danq** of musk. Melt this and stir it until it is blended. Once it is blended by the melting, pierce the head of the statue and pour it inside. Leave it to cool. Once it has cooled, stick a piece of wax over that hole. Then take <margin>9</margin> four **mithqals** of human blood, two **mithqals** of white rooster blood, two **mithqals** of horse brain, and one **danq** each of musk and camphor. Add one **mithqal** of melted fat from a ewe's tail. Gather all of this in a vessel and melt it <margin>12</margin> until it is mixed. Once it is mixed, pierce the statue's collarbone and pour the mixture into it. Then leave it to cool. Once it has cooled, seal it with a piece of wax. Then take a silver nail—it must be thin and never used before—and drive it into the chest of the statue, piercing but not passing all the way through, while you say during the piercing:
> "Akrabous, Ghidayous, <margin>15</margin> Yahilas, Yahidous."
Then place the statue in a new clay jar. When you have finished this, take half a **mithqal** each of powdered frankincense and **kiyya** <note>original: *al-kiyya*, likely a ritual alkali or mineral resin</note>, and the weight of one **mithqal** of a white rooster’s eye. Gather all of this together. Then take the statue, the incense, and a brazier containing fire <margin>18</margin> and go to the peak of a mountain overlooking the land. Dig a hole the size of the statue and bury it upright, with its head facing upwards. Then place a stone or a brick over the top of the jar and return the

### Description of a <term>Nayranj</term> <note>A term for a magical operation or illusion, often involving talismans or chemical recipes.</note> called *Baghyūs*, intended to cause separation and enmity between men and women

Its procedure is that you take fat that has not been used for anything⁶ in such an amount that you can fashion two hollow statues from it in the names of those you wish to separate. Say, "This is the statue of so-and-so [the man]" and "This is the statue of so-and-so [the woman]."⁷ Then take the statue of the man and place it on your palm.⁸ Take the weight of⁹ one <term>danq</term> <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 0.5 grams.</note> of the bile of a black cat, the weight of two **danqs** of pig's bile, the weight of one **danq** of black dog's fat, and the weight of two <term>mithqals</term> <note>A unit of weight equivalent to about 4.25 grams.</note> of black cat's blood. Put all of this into a mixing vessel and place it over a gentle fire until it melts and mixes. Then pour it into his mouth until it reaches his hollow interior. Then take the weight of half a **mithqal** of black dog's fat and the weight of half a **mithqal** of black dog's bile; grind them both together¹² until they are mixed, then pour it into the hole of his collarbone. Then take a thin iron nail and drive it into his chest while saying: "O **Hudīs**¹⁴ **‘Amyālūs**, **Ḥalwānīs**, **Bīhwārās**." Then set him aside by himself until you finish with the other. Then take the other statue and place it on your palm, and take the **Kūz** <note>original: *al-kūz*, likely referring to "blue bdellium" or a similar resin based on the marginal note</note>¹⁶ and the galbanum <note>original: *jāwashīr*</note>, half a **mithqal** of each, and of ammoniacum and aloes...

A magical operation <note>original: "Nayranj"</note> via smoke to cause hatred and separation: Take the brain of an owl and the brain of a bat, one <term>mithqal</term> <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to 4.25 grams.</note> of each; the blood of a red dog and the blood of a black cat, two **mithqals** of each; and pig fat and the brain of a red dog, half a **mithqal** of each. Another smoke to strongly stir the spiritual force: Donkey blood, four **mithqals**; fox blood and hedgehog blood, half a **mithqal** of each. Combine these with one **mithqal** of spurge and use it as a fumigant.

<note>Glossary of technical terms:
**Nayranj**: A magical procedure or mixture using natural properties.
**Mithqal**: A standard unit of weight.
**Fribun**: Euphorbium (spurge).
**Yabruh**: Mandrake.
**Fanajkasht / Habb al-Faqd**: Varieties of the Vitex (Chaste tree) plant.
**Ruhaniyya**: The "spiritual force" or essence believed to reside in substances.
**Talif**: The act of harmonizing or bringing hearts together.
**Hayj**: A state of intense arousal or agitation.</note>

Likewise, the channels of poisons and their spiritual essence are understood through the substances that harmonize, differ, or oppose one another, and their neutralization is also achieved through the spiritual force that repels them.

**The Fourth** of these consists of donkey brain and human fat <note>original: "wadak"; animal or human grease/fat used in medical and magical preparations</note> combined in equal parts. A **daniq's** weight <note>approx. 0.7 grams</note> of it is fed to the subject.

<margin>3</margin> **The Sixth** consists of donkey brain and rabbit blood in equal parts, and an equal amount of animal sweat. It is combined and a **daniq** is fed to the subject.

<margin>6</margin> **The Seventh** consists of black cat brain, bat brain, and hyena fat in equal parts. They are combined by melting and a **daniq** of the mixture is fed to the subject.

**The Eighth** consists of mouse brain and black crow blood in equal parts, plus one-quarter of the total weight in colocynth fat <note>the bitter pulp of the desert gourd</note>. It is combined and a **daniq** of it is fed.

<margin>12</margin> **The Tenth** consists of monkey brain and human brain in equal parts. They are combined by melting and a **daniq** of it is fed.

<margin>15</margin> A **magical operation** <term>Nayranjat</term> to ward off the hands of the world's enemies and their evil from the one who holds it: A frog's heart is placed in its own head and dried. It is held by the person. It is claimed that **Galen** <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note> prepared this compound for a king who lived in his time.

### The Craft of the Indian Bead
This is used by the kings of India and is among the wonders they possess. It repels the harm of poisons and their plots. Its manufacture is as follows: take
<margin>3</margin> the pupils of ten deer eyes and the pupils of ten eyes of vipers or wicked snakes. Their
weights should be equal, whether the number of eyes increases or decreases. Add a weight equal to one of them from the forehead of a whale <note>original: "al-hut"; marginal variants suggest this could also refer to a large fish or even carob ("kharnub")</note>.
Each ingredient is ground separately, and after drying, it is sifted through silk. Then it is gathered and ground 
<margin>6</margin> thoroughly and placed in a glass bottle with a narrow mouth. Then, take one part of citron juice,
one part of radish juice—each part being eight <term>dirhams</term> <note>approx. 3 grams each</note>—and take the weight of one <term>dirham</term> of spider silk, 
clean and white, and one <term>dirham</term> of <term>kayyah</term> <note>original: "kayyah"; likely a caustic or marking substance, or perhaps a typo for mastic ("mastaki") mentioned later</note>. The silk is cut and cast with the mastic into the two aforementioned liquids.
<margin>9</margin> It is left in them for two days and two nights, then strained gently and poured over the pupils. The mouth of the 
bottle is sealed well and buried in a "hay fire" <note>original: "nariyat al-tibn"; a slow, gentle heat produced by fermenting or smoldering straw</note> until the pupils dissolve and become like oil,
mixing with the liquid. Then it is left in that fire until the two aforementioned liquids evaporate and 
<margin>12</margin> only the weight of the pupils remains. It will then be possible to knead it and make it round. It is then placed inside an 
eggshell and rotated until its roundness is perfected. Another shell is applied over it, and it is returned to that fire
until it solidifies slightly. Then, a fine hole is pierced through it, it is wrapped in a silk cloth, and placed inside 
<margin>15</margin> a disc of dough. It is then baked in an oven or placed in the crop of a bird and the bird is roasted. This is done 
to it so that it hardens and becomes a solid stone. Then a thread is passed through it and it is hung on the upper arm.
The kings of India wear it, and the action of this bead is that if poison is present in food, 
<margin>18</margin> drink, perfume, or anything else, that bead twitches, moves, agitates,
and sweats. This is famous among them and is one of the wonders of India.

### The Craft of a <term>Niranj</term> That Kills via Feeding
Dried vitriol, <term>jawz ma’il</term> (datura), black poppy, and colocynth pulp <note>original: "shahm hanzal"; a very bitter and toxic desert fruit</note> in equal parts. The whole is mixed by grinding and placed in the fermentation vessel, then removed 
<margin>9</margin> and stored carefully. The lethal dose is half a <term>daniq</term>. ### Another <term>Niranj</term> That Kills by Acuteness and Corruption of the Heart’s Blood
Hellebore <note>original: "kundus"</note>, euphorbia <note>original: "farbiyun"</note>, and fresh mezereon <note>original: "mazariyun"</note> in equal parts. It is fermented with the gall of a viper equal to the weight of the whole in the vessel prepared for that. Then 
<margin>12</margin> it is removed afterward. Use it to strike, for it takes revenge instantly and does not [merely] kill <note>implying it causes immediate, agonizing death</note>.

### Another Composition That Kills by Rotting and Corruption of the Limbs
Take as many spotted marsh frogs as possible. Iron skewers, like 
<margin>15</margin> rusty and corroded spits, are inserted into their mouths and exited through their rears. They are then placed with their heads facing downward. 
Under these animals, opposite their mouths, lead receivers are placed into which whatever oil drips from them 
descends and collects. This oil, once it has finished collecting and not a single drop remains, 
<margin>18</margin> is that which has no equal. Know that the final drops are the most powerful in action and the most effective in causing harm. This 
compound was first crafted by "Rufus," and he saw from its action that which terrified him. <note>original: "Rufus"; likely Rufus of Ephesus, a prominent 1st-century Greek physician</note>

This king, "Azim," had also constructed in the lands of Nubia a <gloss>3</gloss> bridge at the gate, 
atop which he erected four statues facing the four cardinal directions. In the hand of each statue was 
a bell that would be struck <margin>3</margin> <gloss>a</gloss> whenever a traveler approached from one of those four directions, alerting the people to their arrival. These remained until they were destroyed by the Pharaoh of Moses.

The Indians possess, alongside these deeds, superior <term>Niranjat</term> <note>original: "al-nairanjat," a term for natural magic, sleight of hand, or the manipulation of occult properties of minerals and plants</note> and <term>Talismans</term>. Among these is a technique where a man's member is taken, cut into pieces, and mixed into a powder made of opium, <margin>6</margin> "tilting" nut, and henbane seed. This is then subjected to <term>Putrefaction</term> <note>original: "al-ta'fin," a standard alchemical process of letting a substance decay under gentle heat to transform its essence</note> in a lead vessel. Once removed and preserved, 
this oil—if a tiny amount is placed in food or drink—causes a lethargic trance and prevents 
movement, though without the sleeper actually falling into a natural slumber. They perform wonders with this oil through <margin>9</margin> various applications, adding other substances to it during a meal to create illusions of things they claim are 
supernatural and non-existent. Likewise, they putrefy the flesh of various animals 
and add the milk of spurges <note>original: "yatūʿāt," plants that produce a milky, often toxic or medicinal sap</note> to them. When fed to others, these cause various other illusions and can transform <margin>12</margin> a person, in appearance, into any shape they desire.

They also have rituals involving human sperm. One method involves taking the sperm of a 
perfectly formed man and placing it inside an egg, along with the sperm of any animal they wish to mix <margin>15</margin> 
it with. It is mixed thoroughly, then the egg is sealed, secured, and placed to undergo <term>Putrefaction</term> in a 
heated incubation chamber. After three days, they remove the egg, and within it, a creature resembling 
an animal has formed. It emerges from the egg and is left for three days in the oil of vinegar; <margin>18</margin> 
the creature lives and thrives during these days. Then, they dissolve it while still alive into that oil.

Have a good opinion of yourself in restraining the soul from <term>desire</term> <note>original: "al-hawa," meaning personal whim or base passion</note> and fear the station of your Lord, most High. Direct your desire toward His presence, for the desire of the soul is its seclusion with the beloved and its total inclination <margin>3</margin> toward it. Thus, if its beloved and the object of its longing is the Holy Divine Presence and Lordly care, then the desire is praiseworthy. But if it is toward ephemeral bodies, then it is a blameworthy aim. This is because the path of desire is the path of love, and love is divided: some of it is the love of veneration and magnification, such as the love <margin>6</margin> of God Almighty and the love of fathers and teachers; some is the love of compassion, such as the love of children; and some is the love of benefit, such as the love of the general public and all things from which one gains a benefit. When love becomes excessive, it is called <term>passionate longing</term> <note>original: "'ishq," often implying a consuming or obsessive love</note> and desire. If desire is directed toward other than God, it is the most evil idol ever worshipped. God Almighty shall enlighten your heart to what pleases Him through His expansion of your heart toward His knowledge. Along with this, <margin>9</margin> guard yourself against the commoners and the ignorant among the elite; do not let any of them into any of your secrets, for they are more wicked than predatory beasts, and they are the slayers of the prophets.

I shall mention to you what I saw written by <term>Abu Bishr Matta</term> <note>Abu Bishr Matta ibn Yunus (d. 940), a famous Nestorian Christian philosopher and translator in Baghdad who was a teacher to Al-Farabi</note> in his commentary on the first book of <margin>12</margin> Aristotle's *Metaphysics* <note>original: "Kitab ma ba'd al-tabi'a"</note>. He mentioned "riddles" regarding Aristotle's statement that we must look into the matter of <term>laws</term> <note>original: "al-nawamis," derived from the Greek "nomoi," often referring to divinely inspired laws or social structures</note> and <term>riddles</term> <note>original: "al-alghaz," referring to myths or allegorical teachings</note>. Abu Bishr said: "The extent of the power and greatness of habit is made clear through the matter of the laws, and from them one can deduce the power of habit. For <margin>15</margin> we have been accustomed to proverbs and fables since our youth." Then he said: "If the riddles found in the laws are examined from the perspective of logical proof, they appear as fables, because no proof can be established for them; rather, proof stands for their opposite. But if they are examined from the perspective of the <margin>18</margin> aims of those who established them, they are found to be noble and of great benefit. If they were removed, imagine how the 'prowling of beasts' <note>referring to lawless human behavior</note> would be! For such people comprise most of the world—indeed all of them except for the rare few—to the point that they would destroy both crops and cattle."

## Section (12)

Know, O researcher, that action brings out the secrets of the sciences, and through it, <margin>6</margin> doubts are resolved. For when the knowledge of the desired object is attained, doubts vanish. For this reason, <term>Abu Bishr Matta ibn Yunus</term> mentioned at the beginning of his commentary on the second book of Aristotle's *Metaphysics*—when mentioning what happened between <term>Anushirvan</term> <note>Khosrow I, the famous Sassanid Persian King</note>, King of the Persians, and <margin>9</margin> <term>Mazdak</term> <note>A religious revolutionary in Sassanid Persia, often depicted in later Arabic literature as a heretical trickster</note>—that Mazdak had devised a trick to appear as a prophet. He established a fire temple and built a <margin>12</margin> delicate structure beneath it using materials that fire does not affect at all, such as <term>talc</term> <note>original: "al-talq," likely referring to heat-resistant minerals or asbestos</note> and similar prepared stones. He would put a person inside that place and stand with whomever he wished before the fire, addressing the fire. The fire would then address him and answer him as he wished—but the speaker was the person, not the fire. When Anushirvan heard of this, he found it strange, and his wonder led him to investigate. He demanded that Mazdak show him this, so he stood with him. When the king heard the speech from <margin>15</margin> the fire, he was bewildered. Then, he aimed an arrow toward the source of the speech. The arrow struck the man hiding beneath the grate; the bewilderment ceased, the doubt was resolved, and it became clear to him that the speech did not belong to the fire. 

Abu Bishr did not mention this exactly as I have told it, but rather I saw it in the <margin>18</margin> *History of India* <note>original: "Akhbar al-Hind"</note> in detail. So, O seeker, be stingy with what I have mentioned to you <note>meaning, keep it close and do not share it lightly</note>, and be a faithful guardian of it.

<margin>1</margin> [Nature is] an innate force that constitutes the body and repels corruption from it according to its strength; it provides the body with the benefits of nourishment and other things. <term>Empedocles</term> <note>original: "Banduqlis"</note> said that Nature is a simple substance possessing a single form—meaning it accepts 
<margin>3</margin> forms one by one, a form after the destruction of a previous form, and does not accept them all at once. He also said that Nature contains the power of life, but it is the "image of life," just as a child is a craftsman of all crafts <term>in potentiality</term> <note>original: "bi-l-quwwa," the Aristotelian concept of being able to become something</note>; once he emerges into the world and is trained in a craft, he becomes a craftsman <term>in actuality</term> <note>original: "bi-l-fi'l," the state of being fully realized</note>. We have presented you 
<margin>6</margin> with these treasures so they may spark your understanding and enable you to preserve the causes of things. 
The sage Empedocles said that the causes of substances are four: a cause that exists neither in potentiality nor in actuality but is above them both; a cause in potentiality whose effect is in actuality; a cause in actuality whose effect is 
<margin>9</margin> in potentiality; and a cause in actuality whose effect is in actuality. These are the causes of substances, like our saying: the Will, the Intellect, the Soul, Nature, and the Element. The Will is "in potentiality" with God and "in actuality" with the Intellect; the Intellect is "in potentiality" with the Will and "in actuality" with the Soul; the Soul is "in potentiality" with the Intellect 
<margin>12</margin> and "in actuality" with Nature; and Nature is "in potentiality" with the Soul and "in actuality" with the Element. Thus, each one of these substances is a cause for what is above it in potentiality, and for what is below it in actuality. It is an effect of 
what is above it in actuality, and of what is below it in potentiality. It pours forth virtues upon what is below it and receives them from what is 
<margin>15</margin> above it, <term>emanation</term> <note>original: "fayd," the Neoplatonic concept of light or being flowing from a higher source</note> after emanation, and reception after reception. There are four other causes intermediate between the accidental and the substantial; these are the causes of aims, which are: Inquiry, Gentleness, Love, and that which 
acts of its own essence. Inquiry is for spiritual things that Nature has not sufficed in manifesting; 
<margin>18</margin> Gentleness is for industrial and natural things; while Love and that which acts of its own essence apply to both together. All of these return to Love. God Almighty is the Giver of the perfect emanation to all things, first and last—Glory be to Him, the Most High. Since we have reached this goal, let us make this the end 
<margin>21</margin> of this treatise.

<column-break/>

And reason appears. If we are obliged to thank the father of our birth, how much more should we 
thank the <term>creators of terminology</term> <note>original: "wad'i al-alfaz," those who established the language of science and philosophy</note> through which our life is preserved and our intellects are guarded, along with the existence of the 
<margin>3</margin> <term>Holding Cause</term> <note>original: "al-sabab al-mumsik," the force that keeps a physical body from disintegrating</note> that sustains us. Know, O observer, that in natural bodies there is a power by which they remain, 
preserving their forms and actions, neither moving from them nor changing, for a certain duration specific to each one. Naturalists call this power the "Holding Cause." Through it, bodies 
<margin>6</margin> do not crumble, dissolve, or calcify for a time, but remain in their state and cohesion. 
This is what they express as "Nature." Nature—may God ennoble you—is among the things that must be known. 
Its definition is that it is a primary principle, essentially inherent in every <term>soul</term> <note>some versions omit "soul" here</note> and plant. For example, when a stone falls 
<margin>9</margin> downward, it does not fall merely because it is a "body" (since other bodies differ from it in this), but it falls because of a specific quality 
that distinguishes it from Fire, which extends upward. That quality is the principle for this type of movement 
and is called "Nature." Sometimes the movement itself is called nature, as when it is said: "The nature of the stone is to fall." Sometimes 
<margin>12</margin> it refers to the nature of the element and the essential forms. Doctors apply the name "Nature" to 
the temperament, to the <term>innate heat</term>, to the shapes of the organs, to movements, and to the soul. 
Each of these has its own definition. In reality, it is a <term>homonym</term> <note>a "shared name" applied to different things</note> said of the living, of 
<margin>15</margin> that which is specific to a thing, of the <term>humors</term> <note>original: "al-kymusat" (chymes)</note>, of the world, of the heavens, and of the power which 
the Creator—Mighty and Majestic—made as a cause for the effects of generation, corruption, movement, and rest in every 
moving or resting thing. Therefore, the ancients defined it as "the beginning of movement and rest."

<margin>20</margin> natural substance established for the crafting of things." <term>Galen</term> <note>original: "Jalinus"</note> defined it by a technical definition, saying it is a "heat 
<margin>21</margin> [innate]."

# The Fourth Discourse

We have already completed three discourses of this book, and we are now proceeding to arrange the <margin>3</margin> Fourth Discourse following the previous sequence. In it, I shall mention a portion and examples of the deeds and history of the Nabataeans <note>original: "al-Nabat," ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia often associated in this era with advanced agriculture and occult sciences</note>, the magic of the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note> and the Kurds, and examples of the practice of mechanical-magical tricks. Along with that, I have deposited <margin>6</margin> within this discourse matters of great importance regarding this subject. Upon its completion, the book will be finished. Furthermore, I have not left this book of mine without philosophical discourse through which I may refine your soul.

## Chapter One

Know, O seeker, that the philosophers have agreed that the Creator, may He be exalted, originated five <margin>9</margin> substances. He placed some above others, making the higher ones superior to those beneath them, and characterized them by wisdom, virtues, and light. These five are: the First Matter <term>Hyle</term> <note>original: "al-Hayula al-Ula," the fundamental "stuff" of the universe in Aristotelian thought</note> — which is the Highest World — <margin>12</margin> and the First Form — which is the First Element — then the Intellect, then the Soul, then Nature — which is the Sphere of the Heavens — then the Corporeal Element — which is the Physical Substance. He placed the First Matter at the horizon of His Throne <margin>15</margin> — there is no god but He, glory be to Him — and made it draw light, wisdom, and virtues from Him by means of powers from Him that are compatible with it, transmitting these to it. He then placed the Intellect at the horizon of the First Matter 

<column-break/>

drawing light, wisdom, and virtues from it by means of powers from it that are compatible with it, which transmit these to it. He placed the Soul at the horizon of the Intellect, drawing light, wisdom, and virtues <margin>3</margin> from it by means of powers from it that are compatible with it, which overflow onto it. He placed Nature at the horizon of the Soul, drawing light, wisdom, and virtues from it by means of powers from it that are compatible with it, which transmit these <margin>6</margin> to it. 

Thus, the First Matter is more noble, more delicate, and more subtle than the Intellect; the Intellect is more noble, more delicate, and more subtle than the Soul; the Soul is more noble, more delicate, and more subtle than Nature; and Nature is <margin>6</margin> more noble, more delicate, and more subtle than the Element. He made that which each substance transmits to what is beneath it <margin>9</margin> occur in many successive transmissions, not all at once. It transmits the densest part it possesses so as to be compatible with that which is below it, while its most subtle part remains <note>A Latin translation of this passage notes: "so that the first essence itself may shine more in itself"</note>. This is so that the receiver may long for the giver, needing it, loving it, and never forgetting it. 

Then He originated the celestial spheres and the forms. He placed the Sphere of the Soul between four spheres: <margin>12</margin> two spheres above it that are luminous, virtuous, and refined—namely the First Matter and the Intellect—and two spheres below it that are dark, base, and connected—namely Nature and the Element. Thus, the soul dominated by the two higher spheres is <margin>15</margin> luminous, virtuous, and happy; its destination and resting place is the Highest Paradise from which it was sent forth and from which it drew its strength. But the soul dominated by the two lower spheres is dark, base, and wretched; its destination and resting place is the Lower Fire <note>Hell or the sublunary realm of decay</note> from which it was sent forth and from which it drew its strength. 

He also originated <margin>18</margin> animal, plant, and mineral souls that do not draw from the Intellect or the Higher Matter, for He did not grant them that because they were dominated by the two lower spheres: Nature and the Element. Their destination and resting place is the dust from which they were sent forth and from which they drew their strength. All of this is by the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing. An example of this is that all trees and plants begin with their seed, their origin, and their roots...

...and its end is its branches and twigs, because the Vegetative Soul <term>al-Nafs al-Nabatiyya</term> <note>In medieval philosophy, this is the lowest level of the soul, responsible for basic functions like growth and nutrition shared by all living things.</note> is found in the lower parts of the plant. It draws from the earth through its roots and from the air through its branches. Whichever substance is more abundant in it will prevail. <margin>3</margin> Thus, if the earthy substance is more abundant, the downward growth exceeds the upward in both shortness and width, and vice versa. The proof of this is that we find some plants whose roots are longer than their branches, and some whose branches are longer than their roots. We also find those whose roots have dried up while <margin>6</margin> their branches have not, and those whose branches have dried while their roots have not.

Similarly, if a bird’s nourishment comes mostly from the earth, its upward flight is diminished; but if its nourishment comes mostly from the air, its height is greater. Likewise, when a human’s food is refined and light, they are closer to the spiritual <margin>9</margin> and more capable of attaining simple spiritual things. But if their food is coarse and heavy, they are closer to the corporeal <note>meaning the dense, physical world</note> and more capable of attaining earthly things, yet further from attaining spiritual things. Thus, evil only comes from the corporeal bodies <note>original: "al-ajram," referring to dense physical masses</note>, while good only comes from the spiritual side.

<margin>12</margin> Then let us return to our subject and say: Substance <term>al-Jawhar</term>, in this regard, is divided into two types: spiritual and corporeal. The spiritual includes the First Matter—which is the Highest World—the First Form—which is the First Spiritual Element—the Intellect, the Soul, Nature, the Element, and all <margin>15</margin> the Principles. These are the primary genera which have no species, and the primary indivisible units, such as the number One, the Moment <note>original: "al-An," the indivisible 'now' of time</note>, and the Point <note>the geometric point which has no dimensions</note>, and similar things that cannot be divided. For the Moment is the principle of Time, and the Point is the principle of the Line. Corporeal substance is that which is composed <margin>18</margin> of elements like fire, air, water, earth, animal, plant, and mineral. Substance is also either simple or compound. Simple substance is that which is above...

...the sphere <note>referring to the celestial spheres that surround the Earth in ancient cosmology</note> and is not perceived by the external senses. The compound substance is that which is beneath the sphere and is perceived by the external senses. The sage Empedocles <note>original: "Bunduqlis," a Greek philosopher famous for the theory of the four elements</note> said: "Every substance perceived by the five external <margin>3</margin> physical senses is a purely corporeal, mass-based, compound substance. It is perishable because place encompasses it and boundaries define it. However, every substance that the five external senses cannot perceive, but is perceived by the five internal spiritual senses <note>These were thought to be faculties like imagination, memory, and estimation located in the brain</note>, is a purely simple, spiritual <margin>6</margin> substance. It remains in the light of Lordship forever, never perishing or decaying, because no place encompasses it and no boundary defines it."

Every substance perceived by only *some* of the external senses is a substance positioned between the simple spiritual and the compound corporeal. Whatever part of it is corporeal joins the physical things <margin>9</margin> and perishes with them—such as temporal motion and colors. Whatever part of it is spiritual—such as radiance and light—joins the higher spiritual realm, unites with it, and remains.

Therefore, O you who look into this book of mine, strive to join your soul to the ranks of the spiritually blessed. This will incline you toward <margin>12</margin> the spiritual direction by which you differ from all other beasts: namely, the rational faculty <term>al-Quwwa al-Aqliyya</term>.

Know that the scholars of old and of late have disagreed regarding the true nature of the Intellect <term>al-Aql</term> and its divisions. It is used as a shared term for four meanings. The first <margin>15</margin> is the description by which a human differs from all other beasts; it is the readiness to receive theoretical sciences and to manage subtle, intellectual crafts. It is an innate instinct <note>original: "ghariza"</note> by which the perception of theoretical sciences is prepared. It is as if it were a light that God casts into the heart, by which one becomes ready to perceive things. This is the view of some theologians <term>Mutakallimun</term>. He who <margin>18</margin> denies this and reduces the Intellect to merely "theoretical sciences" has not been fair, for a person who is heedless...

<margin>3</margin> The second division consists of the sciences that emerge into existence within the discerning child through the recognition of what is possible and what is impossible—such as the knowledge that two is more than one, or that a single person cannot occupy two different places at the same time. <margin>9</margin> The fourth division occurs when that innate power reaches the point where it can foresee the consequences of matters; it suppresses the desires that call for immediate pleasure and looks beyond them. <margin>3</margin> Now I command you and present to you something even higher in rank than what I have already mentioned: Know that the ancients divided the intellect into six divisions, summarized by two terms: the "Universal Intellect" and the "Intellect of the All." Similarly, they spoke of the "Universal Soul" and the "Soul of the All." 

The explanation for this is that according to them, existing things fall into <margin>6</margin> three categories: **Bodies**, which are the lowest; **Active Intellects**, which are the most noble because they are free from matter and any connection to it—to the point that they only move matter through desire; and the intermediary **Souls**, <margin>8</margin> which are acted upon by the Intellect and act upon the Bodies. By "Celestial Angels," they mean the souls of the heavenly spheres, for they consider them to be alive. By the "Proximity Angels" <term>al-mala'ika al-muqarrabun</term>, they mean the <margin>9</margin> Active Intellects.

By "Universal Intellect," they mean the "intelligible" concept that is spoken of regarding many individuals who differ in number—specifically, the intellects of individual human beings. This universal has no existence in actual substance or form <margin>12</margin> on its own. For example, if you say "The Universal Human," you are referring to the conceptual meaning of "human" found in all individual persons. This is a single image in the mind that corresponds to all human individuals. There is no <margin>14</margin> single "humanity" that is simultaneously the humanity of Zayd and the humanity of Amr; rather, the mind <margin>15</margin> extracts the image of "human" from a person like Zayd, and it matches all other human individuals. This is called the "Universal Human," and this is what is meant by the "Universal Intellect." <note>original: "quae (scil. ratio) competit omnibus hominibus, et qua ab omnibus aliis animalibus separatur" — This Latin note explains that this reason belongs to all humans and separates them from all other animals.</note>

As for the "Intellect of the All," it is used in two ways. The first—which is most consistent with the literal phrasing—refers to the "All" as the totality of the <margin>18</margin> universe. In this sense, the Intellect of the All refers to the sum total of all essences that are entirely free from matter, which do not move themselves or by accident, but move only through desire. The final rank in this sequence is the Active Intellect, which brings forth the souls...

<margin>3</margin> Furthermore, when the senses are affected by sleep, the soul does not perceive anything. If it is asked why a person might occasionally perceive something in their sleep, the answer is that a remnant of sense-perception remains, just as heat remains in a wick <margin>6</margin> after the lamp has been extinguished. Because of the soul’s union with the body, some have attempted to define its limits. However, **Empedocles** <note>original: "Bunduqlis," the Arabic transliteration for the Greek philosopher Empedocles.</note> claimed that the Intellect <term>al-Aql</term> cannot be defined because it is a "simple substance" <note>A "simple" substance in medieval philosophy is one that is not composed of parts and is therefore indivisible and eternal.</note>. A simple substance has no genus, no species, <margin>6</margin> and no "differentia" <note>The specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus.</note> because it cannot be divided, while the structure of a definition relies on genus, species, and differentia.

He mentioned that there are two types of Intellect: 
1. **The Universal Intellect**, in which all things exist potentially. It neither perishes nor suffers; it is all things in their very essence. It existed before "Eon" <term>al-Dahr</term> <note>Dahr refers to absolute time or eternity, as opposed to "Zaman," which is measured, linear time.</note> and is within its horizon. It is said to be with eternity, not <margin>9</margin> preceding it by even a blink of an eye. 
2. **The Acquired Intellect**, which perishes and suffers. it is only found in the human body; it perishes when the body perishes and suffers when the body suffers. It is a light derived from the light of the Universal Intellect.

He also argued that the Soul <term>al-Nafs</term> cannot be defined because it too is a simple substance. Every simple substance is indivisible; what is indivisible has no genus; <margin>11</margin> what has no genus has no species; what has no species has no differentia. Since the structure of a definition depends on these, that which has no genus cannot be defined. The Soul is only "defined"—despite being a simple substance—because it has united with the body and shone with the light of the Intellect. 

<margin>14</margin> He then mentioned that the Soul is a simple, knowing power that perceives the essence of things. Yet, he also mentioned that it is a "composed substance." **Aristotle** rejected this in the presence of **Plato**, saying: "Everything composed <margin>17</margin> can be dissolved, and whatever can be dissolved can perish. Since you stated it is simple, how can it be composite?" 

Empedocles actually meant a "definition" by the first statement and a "description" by the second. His use of "composed" meant it was composed by the light of the Intellect, not in its own essence. **Plato** and **Syrianus** <note>original: "Sarithlus," likely referring to the Neoplatonist commentator Syrianus.</note> accepted this explanation from Empedocles.

Indeed, we have brought to you, O observer, what we have brought of the discourse on the soul and the intellect and their essences only to pave the way for you and to alert you, so that your sight and your research are focused solely on knowing them. <margin>3</margin> This is so that you may triumph in eternal life and cast aside everything else, for reaching that knowledge is the ultimate goal of perception. This is because the meaning of a shadow is the darkness of an object that stands between the light of the sun and the place directly opposite that object. This occurs during the sun's brightness and its decline, or at its rising until the time it stands at its peak. When the sun stands at its peak, it casts a shadow in all regions according to the <margin>9</margin> latitude and longitude of the land.

In a land that has no latitude, the shadow at the sun's peak appears "inverted" in a person, for shadows can be either "extended" <term>mabsut</term> or "inverted" <term>mankus</term> <note>These are technical terms from medieval Islamic trigonometry and sundial theory. An 'extended' shadow is horizontal, like those on the ground, while an 'inverted' shadow refers to the vertical shadow cast against a wall or measured on an astrolabe.</note>. This is mentioned in the study of the **astrolabe** and engraved upon it. An example of the "inverted" shadow is when we place an object in a kohl-container or <margin>12</margin> against a wall; this has a shadow at every time and in every land.

So, understand what I have pointed out to you. Look with a healing gaze, contemplate with intense research, and reflect, for I have not left anything out that I have not guided you toward. God is the helper to me, to you, and to all our brothers who search for these subtle, <margin>15</margin> obscure, and difficult-to-perceive sciences.

As for the virtuous Sage **Aristotle**, he defined the Soul as: "The perfection of a natural, organic body possessing life potentially." He specified "natural" to exclude artificial bodies. He said "organic" <margin>12</margin> because it enters into those mortal bodies that exist in a state of "coming-to-be and corruption" <note>A classic Aristotelian phrase referring to the material world where things are born and decay.</note> because they require nourishment. He said "potentially" to refer to what has not yet entered into present "actuality."

In a commentary on his *Book of the Soul* <note>original: "Kitab al-Nafs," referring to Aristotle's De Anima.</note> by one of the scholars, it is said that the soul is a "formal cause" for the breathing body; it is through the soul that the body breathes, <margin>15</margin> is nourished, and feels.

**Plato** claimed that the Soul is an "intellectual substance" that moves of its own accord according to a "composed number." He said in another place that the Soul is a substance, not a body, which moves the body and is united with it. Through that union, it connects with material bodies <margin>18</margin> and acts upon them. Some of the ancients defined it as a "nature in permanent motion," and that it is, nonetheless, the perfection of the active body that is "living potentially."

### Drawing Down the Power of the Moon in Taurus

Know that the Moon exerts an influence in each of these zodiac signs, and according to that influence, you should arrange specific works. When the Moon is in **Taurus**, seek out a location as previously described. Bring with you a rooster, as I mentioned to you, and a censer. Then, wear a linen garment dyed with *nairun* <note>original: "النيرون" (al-nairun); likely a reference to a specific dark dye or a chemical preparation used in talismcanic art</note> or pomegranate peel, and pull your sleeve over your head. Draw near to a pot filled with water that has been cooked with walnut wood. Dip your right hand into it, scoop some out, and pour it over your left hand. Wash your hands, your face, and your forearms, taking great care that the sleeve does not slip from your head. Then wash your feet. You must have with you a new mat that no foot has ever stepped upon, encircled with a linen band variegated with green and red. Then, leap from your place into the center of the mat and perform a prostration <term>sajdah</term> upon it. During the prostration, you shall say: *Rabqar, Rabqar, ‘Ayqam, ‘Ayqam, Taqfur, Taqfur* <note>These are "voces magicae" or "names of power." The footnotes suggest variants like "Ribharim" or "Cayphenim" in other versions of the text, such as the Latin Picatrix.</note> twenty times. Then stand up, for a sense of profound humility <term>khushu‘</term> will overcome you until tears flow from your eyes. Approach the pot once more and wash yourself as you did the first time. Then, slaughter your sacrifice and burn it while repeating what I mentioned to you. Throughout all of this, burn frankincense and mastic as incense, for you shall see a figure who will fulfill what you desire. 

Those who occupy themselves with this art claim there was a man whose friend had been oppressed by the hands of time and reduced to poverty. **Saturn** was the lord of his ascendant and the ruler over his deprivation. So, his friend taught him the invocation of the Moon in the sign of **Taurus**. The man saw that spiritual figure and asked for his need; the figure brought him to a graveyard <term>baqi‘</term> and said to him, "Dig here." He dug and found that which restored his condition, moving from deprivation to abundance.

### Drawing Down Its Power in the Sign of Gemini

Seek out a high place where the wind blows. Carry with you your sacrifice, which is a rooster, as well as incense and a copper reed.

### Drawing Down the Moon's Power in the Sign of Cancer

Ascend to an elevated place, such as an upper chamber <margin>16</margin> with a window overlooking an open field where your gaze can stretch far. Look to your right, your left, in front, and behind you. In your hand, <margin>17</margin> hold a turtle-dove or a common pigeon. Slaughter it, then take four feathers from its right wing, <margin>18</margin> four from the other wing, and the same from its tail. Cut off the tip of its breastbone <note>The term "duf" refers to the broad bone of the chest.</note> and burn the rest of it. Take <margin>19</margin> those feathers and add to them two dirhams <note>A dirham is a historical unit of weight, roughly 3 grams.</note> of colocynth fat and four dirhams of liquid storax <term>miah</term>. Combine everything <margin>20</margin> and tie it in a linen cloth. Then, fashion a statue weighing two ounces out of white behen root <note>original: "behmen abyad"; a root used in medieval medicine and magic, often associated with vitality.</note> to which is added

<column-break/>

<page-num>٢٩٩</page-num>

the ash of the sacrifice, kneaded with the water of birthwort <term>zarawand</term>. That statue should be in the form of a man riding a lion. Then, stand <margin>1</margin> with the statue before you and light a fire, offering incense while saying:
> O Moon, who is filled with <margin>3</margin> light, magnificent in beauty, and established in loftiness! To you I raise my desire, and to you I send my petition.

Then, draw a circle on the ground and place the statue in its center after inscribing upon it the name of the one <margin>6</margin> whose affection you desire. Repeat the prayer, then prostrate yourself. Raise your head and take about one pound <term>ratl</term> of vinegar and dissolve the statue entirely within it. Then add to it a grain of musk, a quarter-dirham of ambergris, four <margin>9</margin> dirhams of *suk* <term>a complex compound of perfumes</term>, and half a pound of lupin flour. Place the mixture over a fire until it boils vigorously <margin>9</margin> and thickens. Form it into small cakes <term>aqras</term>, each weighing a quarter-dirham. Set them out under the Moon for seven nights. <margin>10</margin> Then put them away. It is claimed that if you use even one of these as incense for someone to smell, you will achieve your <margin>11</margin> desire from them, whether they be male or female. The author of this craft claimed he tested this during some of <margin>12</margin> his travels in a place full of lions, snakes, and scorpions; they would pass by him and do him no harm.

### Drawing Down Its Power in the Sign of Virgo

Take thirty white starlings <note>original: "zarzur"; a species of bird common in the region.</note>. Slaughter them and cook them with their feathers until they are tender. When you remove them, the feathers will have fallen off. Salt them moderately and set them aside. This must be done thirty days before the Moon enters the sign of Virgo. Then, eat one starling each day after perfuming it with a quarter-dirham <note>A dirham is a unit of weight, approximately 3 grams.</note> of saffron. Do not eat anything else for six hours afterward. Do this every day and be careful to abstain from drinking wine during these days. 

When you have finished this, bathe in the water of an eastern spring. Place half a rotl <note>A historical unit of weight or volume, roughly equivalent to a pint or a pound.</note> of that spring water into a vial you have prepared while the Sun is at three degrees of Pisces and the Moon is at seven degrees of Aquarius. Seal the vial tightly with pitch <note>original: "qir"; bitumen or tar used for waterproofing.</note> that has not been touched by fire. After that, go out to invoke the power of the Moon. Place a censer before you containing *kubbah* <note>original: "al-kubbah"; likely a resinous gum or specific incense blend.</note> and saffron, one ounce of each, in a wide, empty place. Then say: 

> O Moon of beautiful appearance, limitless in giving, high in stature! You by whose light the darkness shines and souls rejoice, and by whose beauty hearts are gladdened, in you is my trust regarding [mention your specific matter].

Then stretch out your left hand toward the vial and say: 

> Afut, Afut

And dig in the ground with your right hand. Every time you dig, repeat that name until...

### Drawing Down Its Power in the Sign of Libra

Gird yourself with a belt made of papyrus ribbon <note>original: "sharit dis"; a ribbon made from water-reeds or papyrus.</note> that grew in water. Go to the bank of an eastern river and present your offering. Walk against the current, watching the Moon, while holding a copper bow you have fashioned. This must be done while Venus is retrograde in Taurus and Mercury is in Aries. Perform this five times, walking back and forth, then cast that bow into the river and say: 

> O glorious and beautiful Moon, to you I have sent it, and for your pleasure I have fashioned it. For you are capable of fulfilling my need and completing my hope.

Then, kindle a fire from the wood of the *daghali* tree <note>A type of thicket or forest wood.</note> and place liquid storax <term>miah</term> within it. Run around the fire at a trot, holding your breath. At the spot where your breath fails, stop and draw a line on the ground from that place toward the fire. Upon that line, write "Ghanayti' Ghanayti'". Then take the soil from where you drew the name and add an equal amount of well-clay <note>original: "tifl al-bi'r"; the fine sediment or clay found at the bottom of a well.</note>. Knead them with still water and fashion two figures: your own image and the image of the one you love. If you desire love, make them embracing. As soon as you finish fashioning them, it shall happen without delay.

## Drawing Down Its Power in the Sign of Sagittarius

<note>Sagittarius is traditionally associated with travel, higher knowledge, and hidden depths.</note>

This is considered by the sages to be difficult to master, as it combines
<margin>12</margin> the work of temples, talismans, and the discovery of treasures. Aim for the time when Mercury is at four
degrees of Cancer. Take ten rotls <note>A rotl is a historical unit of weight; ten rotls would be roughly 5 to 10 pounds depending on the regional standard.</note> of brass and fashion from it five
serpents. Divide the remaining degrees of the sign to complete the five. When they are finished, take them
<margin>15</margin> and go to a clear river. Divert a stream from it and divide that stream into five
smaller channels. Place one serpent in each channel, all of them hollowed out so that the water enters through their tails
and exits through their mouths. Prepare five waterskins and place them at the serpents' mouths. Every time an
<margin>18</margin> hour passes, take that water which the serpents have cast out, leaving them for another hour to pour into the earth,
until the waterskins are filled with that water in this order. Then, take all of it and move to a spot

<column-break/>

about twenty cubits <note>A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm, about 18–20 inches.</note> away from that river. Place the waterskins on the ground and pierce each
skin with a needle. Dig a pit and let the water flow into it. Stand at the time the water is flowing and place
<margin>3</margin> a living snake opposite each waterskin. Then, run quickly to the river and look at the Moon’s reflection in it. Take as much
water as your mouth can hold, run back to the waterskins, and pour it over each skin and snake. Place
a silver censer at the head of each snake and cast into it moist aloeswood, nadd <note>A compound perfume usually made of aloeswood, musk, and ambergris.</note>, and ambergris.
<margin>6</margin> Do not cease the incense until all the water in the waterskins is exhausted. Then, take the snakes, put them
into the skins, and bury them in the pit. Stand over the site, slaughter your sacrificial offering, and perform fifteen
prostrations. Upon raising your head from each prostration, say "Harqum, Harqum" <note>Likely a derivative of the name "Hermes," often invoked in these texts as a source of wisdom.</note> five times.
<margin>9</margin> You will then obtain your need instantly, as a person will manifest to you in the finest form, carrying you
in that very hour wherever you wish, to the East of the earth or its West.

I once had a friend who performed what I have mentioned regarding this sign. That personage came to him,
<margin>12</margin> for his desire was a talisman to extract treasures. The figure carried him to a place no one had ever seen and brought him
a brass image in the shape of an elephant. In its hand was an iron key which it had placed under its feet. He said
to him: "Take this elephant and walk with it wherever you wish. Wherever the key falls from its foot to the ground,
<margin>15</margin> that is the site of a treasure." He took it and had only walked about four cubits when the key fell.
He found a cellar, walked into it, and it led to a magnificent chamber filled with coffins of gold, silver,
and rubies. He took from it what he needed and returned to it as often as he wished.

### Drawing Down Its Power in the Sign of Aquarius

<margin>1</margin> The sages have said that the preliminaries of these works are better than the works themselves; however, when they are combined, it results in the completion of the work that is hoped for. If they are not
<margin>3</margin> combined, there is only exhaustion and the risking of one's soul. There have happened to people who did not master the <term>communion</term> <note>Arabic: *munajat*; an intimate, private prayer or invocation to a spiritual entity.</note> many lessons and wonders that would take long to describe. I have mentioned a portion of this so that you may be cautious; no one should approach this except one whose soul is strong and whose essence is noble. It is claimed that a man was met in the <term>Red Sea</term> <note>original: *Bahr al-Qulzum*</note>
<margin>6</margin> as he was traveling through its deep waters upon the surface of the water itself. It was thought that no one was able to travel there even with ships, let alone upon the surface of the water. He was a man walking faster than a normal stride. He was called out to, but did not answer. The narrator said: "I followed his trail, leaving my own path, and hurried after him. When I nearly caught up to him, he turned his face toward me and said
<margin>9</margin> to me: 'What is the matter with you?' I informed him of the news, and he said to me: 'I have been able to do this for about one hundred
years, along with other things, through communion with the Moon.' Then he said: 'I possess something for whoever wishes to harm me on land
or sea, such that no one can reach me because of it.' I said to him: 'And what is it?' He said
<margin>12</margin> to me: 'This.' He took a handful of water from between his feet with his hand and threw it in front of him. Suddenly, it became a flame of
fire burning whatever it passed by. It moved across the sea in front of me until it disappeared from my sight, dipping
into the water once and appearing another time. He said: 'And thus I do upon the land.' I asked him about that,
<margin>15</margin> and he said to me: 'This is the action of <term>Sarghatum</term> <note>A specific spirit or "servant" associated with the Moon in medieval Arabic grimoires.</note>, the servant of the Moon when it is in the sign of Aquarius.'
If you wish to commune with it in the sign of Aquarius, take the heads of three male geese
and cook them in old wine until they fall apart. Crush them in an iron or lead mortar while the Moon
<margin>18</margin> is in Cancer until it becomes a paste. Add to it half a <term>rotl</term> <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to a pound.</note> of cinnamon, two ounces of sandalwood,
half a rotl of dry liquid storax, a quarter rotl of frankincense, and a little tragacanth. Knead it all together."

[...after several] days, enter it <note>the ritual space</note> wearing a beautiful red garment. The room should have a shutter that you can remove whenever you wish—a board
or something else. Then say: "Hayawum, Hayawum, Bulghar, Bulghar, Naqraw, Naqraw" <note>These are magical names or incantations, likely of Syriac or Hebrew origin, typical of the *Picatrix* tradition.</note>. Then go out and circumambulate

Consequently, a dislike for her fell into the heart of the one who had bought her, and he sent word to him expressing a desire to return her.
<margin>12</margin> The man possessed some cleverness, so he refused to accept her back until he bought her back from him at a low price. The crux of this

<margin>15</margin> It happened in the time of a certain man that he went to draw down the power of the Moon out of ignorance

And these works, according to them, have causes and reasons that would take long to explain; they have inherited them from their ancestors and have practiced these works since ancient times, so take note of that.

The Indians also have works they call <term>phylacteries</term> <note>original: *qalafatiryat*, derived from the Greek *phylakteria*, meaning protective amulets or charms</note>, and these are for the seven planets. Each work they perform is directed toward what the nature of its planet requires. <margin>a) A different version of the following text exists in Paris Arabic MS 2775, folio 165r: "Chapter on the fasting of the planets, their times, and what is said when asking for a need."</margin> For **Saturn**, they observe a fast of seven days, from the day of the Sun <note>Sunday</note> to his day <note>Saturday</note>. > In the name of the King **Ashbayl**, who is appointed over Saturn, by the right of the Master of the Upper Structure <note>A reference to the Creator or the highest celestial sphere</note>, may you carry out my command and fulfill my need.

...with the wine in which the heads <note>presumably animal heads mentioned in the preceding text</note> were cooked. Make forty cakes from that and fry them in an iron pan until they dry. Then go out with them to the open field on a moonlit night while the **Moon is in Aquarius**. Place before you fifteen censers made of brass and silver—and if you are able to have some of gold, then do so, otherwise these will suffice. Cast into each censer one of those cakes and offer your sacrifice. At the moment the smoke rises, you will see a figure appearing sometimes and vanishing at others. Take three of the cakes and cast them into the fire toward him, then say: "*Hantar Asrak, Hantar Asrak*" ten times. He will then come to you and teach you what will benefit you.

### Drawing Down Its Power in the Sign of Pisces

Extract the juice of Nabataean cauliflower. Take a portion of it weighing one <term>rotal</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 1 pound</note> and one-fifth of a rotal of lettuce juice, and a little taro juice. Mix these and extract them while the **Sun is in Virgo and Mercury is direct**, using a marble mortar. Add to it four <term>dirhams</term> <note>a small unit of weight</note> of mastic, two dirhams of ambergris, two dirhams of camphor, an ounce of sugar, and ten dirhams of sarcocolla <note>original: *anzarut*, a resin used in traditional medicine</note>, after grinding what needs to be ground. Add half a rotal of the blood of a fawn slaughtered with a brass knife. 

When it is all mixed, place it in a glass vessel. Then go to a place where there is a water spring. Place the glass vessel on the edge of the water and take a censer you have prepared with you; place it on a rock in the middle of the spring with the water surrounding it. Kindle a fire in it, and when it is lit, open the mouth of the vessel and place a little of its contents into the censer, bit by bit, time after time. Offer him your sacrifice, for this incense will bring to you the **Servant of the Moon** in this sign. Ask him for your need, and he will grant you your desire.
