In the world of the **Rational Animal** <note>original: "al-hayawan al-natiq," a classic Aristotelian definition of a human being</note>, over which all that we have mentioned is disposed however it wills and which has been granted the right of discernment. This entire world, in its entirety, is under the governance of the **Elements** <term>Istiqqasat: from the Greek 'stoicheia', referring to earth, air, fire, and water</term>. The Elements are under the governance of **Nature**, Nature is under the **Soul**, the Soul is under the **Intellect**, and the Intellect proceeds from the **Creator**—exalted be His name—for He is the one from whom grace flows upon it and upon all.

Here, "from" refers to the **Agent** <note>the active cause</note>, not the **Material**—like a pitcher is made "from" brass, meaning brass is its material. Nor does it mean He is merely a cause for it, but rather that He is the active Agent. Understand this well.

And you, O reader who examines what we have deposited in this our book, must pray for us. We have excerpted for you the best of what the people <note>referring to ancient sages and scholars</note> mentioned in their books, not out of greed or stinginess on our part, as those who came before may have done. Therefore, we saw fit that this book should not be devoid of the **Secrets of the Nabataeans** <note>The Nabataeans were an ancient Semitic people; here, the text refers to the occult and agricultural traditions attributed to them</note> which this man, **Ibn Wahshiyya** <note>A famous 9th-century scholar known for translating works on magic and agriculture from Syriac/Nabataean into Arabic</note>, translated from them. Furthermore, because of the greatness and nobility of this book in existence, I have mentioned its obscure points to you and spared you the need for deep investigation or the exertion of thought. May God bring you to your desires.

**Snakes** flee from the scent of **elk horn**, and **ants** flee from the scent of 
**cumin**. The **gecko** flees from **saffron** so that it does not shelter in any place where 
it is found. The **flea** flees from **quicklime** <note>original: "al-nura," a caustic chemical made from burnt limestone</note> if it is spread on the ground of a place, and it also flees 
from **marsh salt** if it is spread heavily in houses. The **bedbug** flees from **germander** <note>original: "al-ja'da," a bitter medicinal herb</note> 
if it is used as a strong incense.

**Moss** <note>original: "al-tahlab," referring to water-moss or algae</note> is not affected by fire at all, and **jujube wood** has never been seen to produce 
a flaming or glowing fire.

The **eagle** <note>original: "al-nasr," which can refer to an eagle or a vulture in medieval Arabic</note> protects its chicks in its nest from **bats** using **plane tree leaves**, which it spreads 
in its nest because the bat perishes from the scent of the plane tree.

The **Tiraz stone** <note>original: "hajar al-tiraz," perhaps referring to a decorative or "embroidered" stone</note> is among those things that cannot be divided; it is a stone whose small or 
large pieces cannot be broken. The stone found in the **Egyptian Nile** is carved in the shape of a boat; one can cross in it 
from one side to the other. It is a stone weighing thousands of pounds <note>original: "artal," a traditional unit of weight</note> that stays atop the water and does not sink.

The **Amethyst stone** <note>original: "al-jamast"</note>, if a number of pieces are placed in cups and wine is drunk from them, the drinker will 
not become intoxicated. The **Tabari stone**, if a number of pieces are thrown into a goblet and then 
wine is drunk from it, causes powerful intoxication, takes away the mind, and induces obsessive whispering <note>original: "al-waswas," often implying anxiety or madness</note>. The **Magnetite stone** <note>original: "al-maghnitis"</note> 
attracts iron, but if it is rubbed with **garlic**, it will no longer attract it; however, if it is placed in **goat's blood**, its power of attraction returns.

The **Eagle Stone** <term>Hajar al-Uqab: also known as Aetites, a hollow stone with another stone inside it</term> is a red stone the color of Cypriot clay. A stone moves inside 
it, but if it is broken, nothing is found in its core. It eases childbirth for pregnant women.

The **Salamander** <note>original: "al-salamandriya"</note> is an animal in the shape of a small fox with the legs of a 
large weasel. It extinguishes fire with its coldness, and its skin is not affected by fire. The

its belly and melts.

**Feathers** from any bird: if one makes a medium-sized shape from them and rubs it continuously against a garment or with the hand many times, 
then brings it near any small body, it will lift it with force <note>An early observation of static electricity</note>.

The **Dazzling Stone** <note>original: "al-hajar al-bahat"</note> is a stone the color of **marcasite**. it glitters beautifully; if a 
human sees it, they laugh until they die. Nothing can cure them of this, even if they are shielded from it after seeing it.

The **Porphyrio** <note>original: "al-farfir," likely the purple gallinule</note> is a bird in the image of a sparrow, black with a red collar and red eyes, 
as well as red legs. If it lands upon the Dazzling Stone, it nullifies its effect, and a human may then look at it 
without harm.

The **Peony** <note>original: "al-fawiniya"</note> is an Ethiopian wood. If broken, its cross-section always reveals a cross. Likewise, 
if the broken piece is broken again into the smallest possible pieces, this image remains—one of the wonders 
of Nature's handiwork—as it consists of four opposing circles. If hung upon those with **epilepsy**, it 
cures them through the constant inhalation of its scent.

The **Harai Tree** <note>original: "shajarat al-harai," likely referring to a species of Mandrake or a similar narcotic plant known in Persian lore</note>, also known as the **Short Tree**, is from Khurasan. There are male and female varieties. If five **dawaniq** <note>a unit of weight; one daniq is approximately 0.5 grams</note> of the female variety is given to women to drink, they are overcome by an uncontrollable arousal and cast their veils behind their backs. 
<margin>3</margin>If a person drinks five dawaniq of the male variety, the penis remains erect and does not subside unless the drinker takes two **dirhams** <note>about 3 grams</note> of **bamboo manna** <term>tabashir: a silica-rich medicinal substance found in the joints of bamboo</term>, which dissolves the effect. As for the seeds of the male tree, if 
any of them are crushed into a person's food, they will suffer from uncontrollable flatulence from the 
<margin>6</margin>moment they eat it until it is fully digested in the stomach, and there is no escape from it. If a small amount of the female seeds is given 
to a person with wine, they will sleep for three days; the remedy is to give them hot water 
and **rikabi oil** <note>a high-quality oil, often sesame or olive, traditionally transported by camel caravans</note>. The leaves of this tree, when ground and kneaded with dissolved sulfur water, 
<margin>9</margin>cure **leprosy** <term>al-baras: can refer to leprosy or vitiligo in medieval texts</term> in a single day with just one application.
The wood of the **Frankincense tree** <note>original: "al-kundur"</note>, if it falls upon snakes or scorpions, they die 
instantly and suddenly. 
<margin>12</margin>**Salt** is beneficial for the stings of scorpions and wasps and the bites of snakes. **Purslane** <note>original: "al-baqla al-hamqa'," literally "the foolish herb"</note> 
stops hemorrhaging and is effective for coughs within one or two days if eaten continuously. 
The **goat**, if it senses a **lion**, dies a natural death. If the hair of the sheep is taken while it is 
<margin>15</margin>in that state, clipped with scissors using the left hand, and used as incense for someone suffering from **quartan fever** <note>a fever associated with malaria that recurs every four days</note>, 
it cures them that very day; however, the fever may return more severely than its usual habit before finally ceasing.

<column-break/>

**Sulfur** kills every body, burns it, and causes it to "die," yet it "revives" **gold**, improves it, 
refines it, and increases its beauty. **Malachite** <note>original: "al-dahnaj"</note> also softens gold, removes its brittleness, and makes it 
<margin>3</margin>pliable when smelted with it. If mixed with **borax** <note>original: "al-tinkar," an alchemical flux</note>, it works even faster. The pressed water of **henna**, 
if poor-quality gold is heated and quenched in it repeatedly, makes the gold very soft. **Salt** increases 
the redness of gold excessively. As for **silver**, if it catches the scent of sulfur, it turns black; but if 
<margin>6</margin>salt touches it, it turns white and pure.
The property of **Sal Ammoniac** <note>original: "al-nushadir"</note> is to draw things out from their depths and heights. **Natron** <note>original: "al-natrun," a natural soda salt</note> 
washes bodies of grime and brightens their "faces" <note>the surface appearance of metals</note>. **Lapis Lazuli**, when combined with gold, 
<margin>8</margin>increases its beauty, and if thrown upon embers without a flame, it produces a "tongue of fire." **Obsidian** <note>original: "al-sabaj," could also refer to jet</note> 
and its effect on the eyes [is significant]. **Marcasite** <note>original: "al-marqashina"</note>, if its sulfur is burnt away and it is calcined until it is white like flour, becomes

# A Talisman to Gather Fish
Let millet <note>original: "al-jawars," a type of small-grain broomcorn</note> ferment, then add goat fat, crushed fava beans, and bull’s blood. Mix until the whole becomes a single mass, then place it in a reed basket and tie it with a hemp thread.
<margin>3</margin> Then, place it in a location where you know there are fish. No fish that catches its scent will remain; they will all gather toward it. Then, cast your net and take them all.

# A Fumigant Talisman to Smoke Trees
So that no bird remains without falling when it catches the scent:
<margin>6</margin> Take equal parts sea turtle fat, Egyptian indigo seeds, galbanum <note>original: "jawashir," a medicinal gum resin</note>, and hellebore <note>original: "kundus," likely white hellebore, known for causing sneezing and dizziness</note>. 
Crush them all and knead them with donkey urine. Dry it in the shade after forming it into pills the size of chickpeas. 
Keep them, and when you wish to work, place one pill on charcoal fire under a tree containing birds. Plug 
<margin>9</margin> your nose with cotton, for if the birds smell the scent, they will become intoxicated and fall. If you wash their feet 
with hot water, they will recover immediately.

# Another Fumigant Talisman for the Same Purpose
Take equal parts of *yaruh* and *qashir* <note>likely local names for specific aromatic plants or minerals</note> and knead them with the juice of a fresh 
<margin>12</margin> wild rue <term>harmal: a plant used extensively in Middle Eastern folk magic to ward off the evil eye</term> tree. Form it into chickpea-sized pills and dry them. Smoke the birds with it, but do not do so on a 
windy day, for the wind will scatter the smoke. When you finish your work, smoke the tree with the fragrance of 
frankincense and costus <term>qust: a fragrant root used in ancient perfumes and incense</term> to remove this foul smell from the tree.

# A Talismanic Crown: Whoever Wears It, His Sight is Brightened
Until he can see things from a great distance. 
<margin>15</margin> When he removes the crown from his head, his state returns to how it was before. Take branches of a tree 
called *qatla* <note>original: "qatla," likely the Strawberry Tree (Arbutus unedo)</note> while they are still fresh and supple. Fashion a crown from them and wear it; it will do what we have mentioned. 
<margin>18</margin> The juice of this tree is of great benefit when mixed with wine vinegar; if applied to leprosy <note>original: "al-baras," often referring to vitiligo or white skin patches in historical texts</note>, it 
heals it quickly.

# A Talisman: A Bell to Drive Snakes and Scorpions from Their Holes
Take "Pharaonic glass" <note>likely refers to high-quality ancient glass or lead glass</note> 
and steel filings, and melt them in a crucible. Feed it <note>an alchemical term for adding a substance to a molten mix</note> red arsenic and red magnesia. 
<margin>3</margin> Then take it out and break it into small pieces. Take the head of the "Coptic raven" found in Egypt with its bones and crush it 
with black galbanum. Then "feed" it to the iron while it is melted once more. Then, fashion a bell <term>juljul: a small spherical crotal bell with a loose pellet inside</term> from it. 
Its pellet <note>the loose piece inside the bell that makes it ring</note> should be made of lodestone <term>maghnitis: natural magnetic iron ore</term>. When you have finished, strike it at the door of 
<margin>6</margin> the holes of snakes, scorpions, or similar creatures. They will come out, and you may do with them as you wish. The maker of this 
is Agathodaimon <note>original: "Agathidimun," the "Good Spirit," a legendary figure in Hermetic and alchemical tradition often depicted as a serpent</note>. This bird <note>referring back to the raven used in the recipe</note> possesses a property such that when it cries out, all snakes come out and drop dead 
from its cry.

# A Fumigant Talisman to Gather Mice to One Place
Take the juice of the white vine <note>original: "karmah bayda," possibly white bryony</note>, 
<margin>9</margin> the juice of a "mouse-onion" <term>basal al-far: the sea squill, used historically as a rodenticide</term>, borax, and red Indian cowpeas. Crush the cowpeas and the borax and knead them 
with the juices. Form them into chickpea-sized pills and dry them in the shade. Keep them, and smoke one pill on 
<margin>12</margin> glowing embers. The mice will gather to the smoke, and you can do with them what you intend.

# A Talisman to Gather Crabs
Take the leaves of the *qaydārūs* tree <note>possibly a corruption of "cedrus" (cedar) or a specific aromatic plant</note>, the leaves of the 
"fox-plant" <note>original: "shajarat al-tha'lab," likely nightshade or foxglove</note>, and rabbit blood. Crush them all and form them into a ball. Tie it in a cloth and lower it by a thread 
<margin>15</margin> into a place in the water where there are crabs. they will gather to the medicine and cling to it until not a single one 
is left.

### Talisman for a cup that prevents the drinker from getting drunk
You should make a cup of *taliqon* copper <note>original: "nahas al-taliqun," likely an alchemical alloy or "white copper"</note> of a slight thickness. Prepare citron-leaf vinegar, distilled using a cucurbit and alembic <note>standard alchemical distillation equipment</note>, juice of Nabataean cabbage, and juice of fresh nut grass <note>original: "su'd," likely Cyperus rotundus</note> in equal parts. Mix them. Then, heat the cup before polishing it and quench it in this mixture. Heat it again and quench it until it has "drunk" about a pint of the liquid. Then, polish it and keep it with you. When you wish to use it, coat it lightly with bitter almond oil, then give it to someone to drink from, or drink from it yourself; for whoever drinks from it shall never become intoxicated.

### Talisman to be placed on the dining table
So that no flies ever land on it: Take fresh frankincense, yellow arsenic <term>orpiment: a yellow mineral once used as a pigment and in magic</term>, and dried truffle. Combine them by crushing and mixing, then knead them with the juice of a squill <note>original: "unṣul," a medicinal sea onion</note>. Grease your hands with oil and fashion from it a shape like a talisman. Place it on the table, and no flies will approach it as long as it remains there.

### Another Talisman
This is for making a leather mat <term>sufra: a traditional circular leather or cloth mat used as a dining surface</term> that no vermin will ever approach: Take the skin of a *yamur* <margin>The *yamur* is a wild animal of the "Great Eye" <note>likely referring to a specific species of deer or gazelle mentioned in classical zoology</note></margin> and tan it as hide is tanned. Make a dining mat from it, and it will perform as we described. This has been witnessed and confirmed; such skins are sold currently in Mecca.

### An inky talisman for snakes
Crush round birthwort <note>original: "zarawand mudahraj," a medicinal plant used in antiquity for snake bites</note> and add it to the meat of a wild frog. After crushing it well, add black ink to it so it is mistaken for regular ink. Dry it in the shade after forming it into pellets. When needed, dissolve a pellet in ammonium chloride water <note>original: "ma' al-nashadir"</note> and write whatever you wish—words that cannot be recognized—on both sides of a piece of paper. Then, toss it into the basket of a snake-charmer <term>al-hawi: a professional snake handler or street performer</term>.

### A smoky talisman
When used as a fumigant, a vapor rises to the sky resembling fire, causing fear. Take the root of the "Demon's Lamp" herb <note>original: "saraj al-qutrub," possibly mandrake or a bioluminescent plant</note>—which is seen at night as if it were a lamp. Grind it and knead it with the brain of a deer and the gallbladder of a bull. Form it into pellets the size of chickpeas and dry them in the shade. Then, burn it over a fire made of dung. A wondrous vapor will rise from it, appearing like a red fire in the sky, so that people become terrified. This only works in cloudy weather and turbulent air.

### A lamp talisman
Whoever holds it in his hand will not be able to see, as his vision is dimmed by its light, yet whoever stands behind him will see everything in the house by its radiance: Take the fat of a fish called *al-dukhas*, known in Egypt as the dolphin. Melt it until it becomes oil, then store it. When ready to work, make a wick from a linen rag and coat it in crushed verdigris <note>original: "zanjār," a green pigment from weathered copper</note>. Then light it with that oil in a copper lamp, and what we described shall occur.

### A talisman which, if placed under a sleeping person's head,
Will cause them not to sleep at all, but remain awake and restless until it is removed: Grind the herb maidenhair fern <note>original: "barshawushan"</note>, sift it, and knead it with the milk of a nursing sow. Fashion from it the image of a boy who looks as if he is having a seizure. If this is placed under a person's head, his mind will be distracted, and he will stay awake and not sleep.

### A talisman which, if a man ties it to his waist
And has intercourse, no child will be born to him; he will remain so as long as it is tied to his waist: Fashion an image of a monkey out of copper and pierce its back...

<margin>3</margin> **Talisman**: This is the process for making "red water" to be poured into lamps, so that the house and everything in it appears as if it were shimmering red rubies. Roast green Cypriot vitriol <term>qalaqant: a metallic sulfate used in alchemy and dyeing</term> in a heated oven for one night. If it turns red, it is ready; if not, repeat the process. Once it has turned red, grind it and add five times its weight in distilled wine vinegar. Place it in a thick glass bottle and leave it for three days, shaking it
<margin>6</margin> three times each day. Then filter it; there will emerge from it a red water like purple dye. Place it in the lamps and you will see a marvel.
<margin>9</margin> **Another Talisman** similar to it, used for lighting to appear like purple: Take one part of dry lime and one part of "dyers' roots" <note>original: "urooq al-sabaghin," likely refers to Madder or a similar plant used for red dye</note>. After grinding them, pour four times their volume of water over them. Put the mixture in a pot and boil it gently, then let it cool and filter it. A red water will come out
<margin>12</margin> like a ruby, shimmering beautifully.
**Talisman** for the creation of deadly green scorpions: Fast for one day, and at the end of the day, chew leaves of wild basil <term>badhruj: an aromatic herb, often Ocimum basilicum</term>. Place the chewed leaves in a glass flask and seal its opening tightly. Hang it in a dark, damp room where the sun does not enter. After forty days, green scorpions will be generated
<margin>15</margin> within it. If they sting a person, they will kill them. There is also a benefit in them: if they are submerged in oil and hung in the sun for twenty-one days until they dissolve and die, it becomes a medicine for scorpion stings.

# The Picatrix

<image-desc>A horizontal sequence of seven white planetary sigils or magical characters on a black background. These symbols correspond to the seven classical planets as depicted in the Picatrix tradition: a crescent moon for the Moon, a forked symbol for Mercury, a horizontal bar with a triangle for Venus, a circle for the Sun, a stylized double-curve for Mars, a symbol with horizontal lines and loops for Jupiter, and a keyed symbol with small circles for Saturn.</image-desc>

->or<-

## The Goal of the Wise <note>Original titles: "Ghayat al-Hakim" (Arabic) and "Das Ziel des Weisen" (German).</note>

->of<-

->Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti / Pseudo-Magriti <note>Maslama al-Majriti (died c. 1007 CE) was a famous mathematician and astronomer from Madrid (al-Majrit). ### And here the book concludes. Praise be to God, the Giver and the One who favors us with 
### Intellectual Light <term>al-nur al-aqli: In medieval philosophy, this refers to divine illumination—a gift from the Creator that allows the human mind to understand universal truths and the secrets of the cosmos.</term> without end. ### May His blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, his family, and all his companions.

---

The book **The Goal of the Wise** <note>original: "Ghayat al-Hakim," the influential grimoire of astral magic known in the Latin West as the *Picatrix*.</note> is a comprehensive compendium of Hellenistic, Near Eastern, and Indian magical traditions. It focuses on the intersection of astrology and talismanic magic, positing that a practitioner can harness the celestial influences of the planets by creating specific objects at precise astronomical moments. This concluding page reflects the medieval tradition of framing even "hidden" or "occult" sciences within a religious context, attributing the ability to perform such wonders to the "Intellectual Light" granted by the Divine.

<summary>This page concludes the manuscript of the Picatrix, providing the formal titles, attribution to the 10th-century scholar al-Majriti, and a closing religious dedication. It serves as both a title page and a colophon, framing the magical content of the book as a branch of divinely-granted knowledge.</summary>

<keywords>Picatrix, Ghayat al-Hakim, Maslama al-Majriti, Pseudo-Magriti, astral magic, planetary sigils, Intellectual Light, colophon, Arabic occultism</keywords>

<term>Picatrix</term>: The Latinized title of the work, which became its most common name in the Western world.

<term>The Goal of the Wise</term>: A literal translation of the original Arabic title, *Ghayat al-Hakim*, emphasizing that magic is the highest form of wisdom.

<term>Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti</term>: A 10th-century Andalusian polymath to whom the work was traditionally, though likely incorrectly, attributed.

<term>Planetary seals</term>: Esoteric symbols used in ritual magic to represent and harness the power of the seven classical planets.

<term>Grimoire</term>: A textbook of magic, typically including instructions on how to create magical objects like talismans and how to perform spells.

## **The Goal of the Wise** <note>original: "Ghayat al-Hakim" (Arabic) and "Das Ziel Des Wiesen" (German). Both titles translate to "The Goal of the Wise." This title suggests that the knowledge contained within represents the ultimate culmination of study for a "wise man" or philosopher—specifically one seeking to master the hidden mechanics of the universe. The original transcription included a German spelling error, "Wiesen" (meadows) instead of "Weisen" (wise).</note>

->of<-

### Maslama ibn Ahmad al-Majriti / <term>Pseudo-Majriti</term> <note>Maslama al-Majriti (died approximately 1007 CE) was a famous mathematician and astronomer from Madrid in Islamic Spain. While the book was traditionally attributed to him to give it intellectual authority, modern scholars believe it was written by an anonymous author in the mid-11th century, hence the designation "Pseudo-Majriti" (meaning "falsely attributed to Majriti").</note>
